lessons.title: Roots and the Root System
lessons.notes_html:
The Root System and Shoot System

The root system is the underground part of the plant; it absorbs water and minerals and anchors the plant in the soil. The shoot system is the aerial part above the ground — stem, branches, leaves, flowers and fruits — which prepares food and bears the reproductive parts.

Primary and Secondary Roots

The primary root is the first root that grows out of the seed when it germinates. It grows straight down into the soil and gives rise to the secondary (lateral) roots. It anchors the plant firmly and absorbs water and minerals from deep in the soil. The secondary roots are the side branches of the primary root; they spread out in the soil in different directions, increase the area of absorption and help to hold the plant firmly in the ground.

Internal Structure of the Root

The epidermis is the outermost layer of cells of the root; it protects the inner tissues and root hairs arise from it. Root hairs greatly increase the surface area for absorption of water and minerals. The root cap is a protective cap of cells covering the tip of the growing root; it protects the tender tip from injury as the root pushes through soil particles. The endodermis is the innermost layer of the cortex, lying just outside the vascular tissue, and it controls the entry of water and salts into the xylem. The cortex between them stores food.

Key Points

  • The primary root grows straight down from the seed; secondary roots branch out from it.
  • Root hairs absorb water and minerals; the root cap protects the growing tip.
  • The endodermis controls the entry of water and salts into the xylem.

mcqs.why: The endodermis is the innermost layer of the cortex, lying just outside the vascular tissue, and it controls the entry of water and salts into the xylem.

mcqs.why: The primary root is the first root to emerge from the germinating seed; it grows straight down and later gives rise to the secondary roots.

options: roots growing out of the stem
side branches that arise from the primary root
mcqs.why: Secondary (lateral) roots branch out from the primary root, spread in the soil, increase the area of absorption and hold the plant firmly.

mcqs.why: Root hairs are outgrowths of the epidermal cells of the root; the epidermis is the outermost layer and also protects the inner tissues.

mcqs.why: The many thin root hairs present a huge surface to the soil, so the root can absorb much more water and dissolved minerals.

mcqs.q: The underground part of the plant that absorbs water and anchors it is the:
mcqs.why: The root system is the underground part of the plant; the shoot system (stem, leaves, flowers) is the part above the ground.

mcqs.why: The endodermis lies just outside the vascular tissue and acts as a checkpoint controlling which water and salts pass into the xylem.

options: spreading in the soil, increasing absorption and holding the plant firmly
mcqs.why: By branching in different directions, secondary roots cover more soil, absorb more water and minerals and anchor the plant strongly.

mcqs.why: The primary root grows straight downwards, reaching deep soil water and giving rise to the secondary roots as it grows.

lessons.title: Transport in Plants: Xylem, Phloem and Transpiration
lessons.notes_html:
Xylem and Phloem

Xylem conducts water and dissolved minerals from the roots up to the leaves through the stem. Phloem transports prepared food from the leaves to the roots and all other parts of the plant. Together xylem and phloem form the vascular bundles, the transport system of the plant: without them, distant parts of a tall plant could not receive water and food.

Diffusion and Osmosis

Diffusion is the movement of molecules from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, and it can take place in any medium. Osmosis is the diffusion of water only, through a semi-permeable membrane, from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution.

How Water Rises: Capillary Action and Transpiration Pull

Capillary action is the rise of water in very narrow tubes (xylem vessels) due to cohesion between water molecules and adhesion with the walls. Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of a living plant, mainly through the stomata of leaves. It is different from evaporation, which is the change of water into vapour from any open surface and is a simple physical process. The evaporation of water from the leaves produces a pulling force — the transpiration pull — which draws the whole water column upwards from the roots.

Factors Affecting Transpiration

Wind sweeps away the humid air around the leaves, so transpiration increases in wind. Rise in temperature increases the rate, and in light the stomata remain open so transpiration is faster in sunlight. Humid air already contains much water vapour, so the rate of transpiration decreases as humidity increases; it is rapid in dry air. Transpiration also cools the plant and keeps the cells turgid.

Key Points

  • Xylem carries water and minerals upwards; phloem carries prepared food to all parts.
  • Osmosis is the diffusion of water through a semi-permeable membrane.
  • Capillary action and transpiration pull together raise water to the top of tall trees.
  • Transpiration decreases when the humidity of air increases.

mcqs.q: Water and dissolved salts are conducted from roots to leaves by:
mcqs.why: Xylem vessels conduct water and dissolved minerals from the roots up through the stem to the leaves; phloem carries prepared food instead.

mcqs.q: Prepared food is transported from the leaves to the other parts of the plant by:
mcqs.why: Phloem transports the food prepared in the leaves to the roots, stem, flowers and fruits for growth and storage.

mcqs.q: The loss of water from the aerial parts of a plant is called:
mcqs.why: Transpiration is the loss of water as vapour from the aerial parts of a living plant, mainly through the stomata; evaporation is loss from any open surface.

mcqs.q: The force between the molecules of water is the:
mcqs.why: Cohesion is the attraction between molecules of the same substance (water molecules); adhesion is the attraction between water and the xylem walls.

mcqs.q: The rate of transpiration decreases with the increase of:
mcqs.why: Humid air already holds much water vapour, so diffusion of vapour out of the leaf slows down and transpiration decreases.

mcqs.q: Osmosis is the movement of:
mcqs.why: Osmosis is the diffusion of water only, through a semi-permeable membrane, from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution.

mcqs.q: The rise of water in very narrow xylem vessels is due to:
mcqs.why: In very narrow tubes water rises by capillary action, caused by cohesion between water molecules and adhesion with the tube walls.

mcqs.q: Transpiration pull is produced when:
options: roots push water up by force
water evaporates from the leaves, drawing the water column upwards
mcqs.why: As water is lost from the leaves, a pull is created at the top of the plant which draws the continuous column of water up from the roots.

mcqs.q: Transpiration becomes faster when:
mcqs.why: Higher temperature gives water molecules more energy to evaporate, so the rate of transpiration increases; humidity and closed stomata slow it down.

mcqs.q: Vascular bundles of a plant are made of:
mcqs.why: Vascular bundles are the plant's transport system, made of xylem (water and minerals) and phloem (prepared food).

lessons.title: Photosynthesis
lessons.notes_html:
What is Photosynthesis?

Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food. Carbon dioxide and water combine in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll to produce glucose and oxygen.

Word equation: Carbon dioxide + Water → Glucose + Oxygen (in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll).

Requirements and Products

In addition to light, photosynthesis requires carbon dioxide and water. Its products are glucose (food) and oxygen, which is released as a by-product. Chlorophyll, the green pigment present in the mesophyll cells of the leaf, traps the light energy. Magnesium is the mineral required for the formation of chlorophyll; without it the leaves turn yellow. Nitrogen (taken in as nitrates) is needed to make proteins for growth and for building new cells and enzymes.

How the Leaf is Adapted

The leaf is broad and flat, giving a large surface to absorb maximum sunlight, and thin, so gases diffuse in and out quickly. Its mesophyll cells contain many chloroplasts. Stomata on the lower epidermis let carbon dioxide enter and oxygen leave, while veins bring water and carry away the prepared food. The spongy mesophyll, with its air spaces, allows gases to diffuse through the leaf.

Proving that Oxygen is Produced

Twigs of Hydrilla are placed under an inverted funnel in a beaker of water, with a water-filled test tube over the funnel stem, in sunlight. Gas bubbles collect in the tube, and the gas relights a glowing splint — the test for oxygen — proving that oxygen is produced during photosynthesis.

Key Points

  • Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using sunlight and chlorophyll.
  • Chlorophyll is found in mesophyll cells; magnesium is needed to form it.
  • The leaf's broad, flat, thin shape and its stomata adapt it for photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: What is required for photosynthesis in addition to light?
mcqs.why: Photosynthesis combines carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll to make glucose, releasing oxygen.

mcqs.q: Oxygen and ________ are the products of photosynthesis:
mcqs.why: The food product of photosynthesis is glucose; oxygen is released as a by-product. Carbon dioxide and water are the raw materials, not products.

mcqs.q: Chlorophyll is present in:
mcqs.why: The mesophyll cells of the leaf contain many chloroplasts with the green pigment chlorophyll, which traps light energy.

mcqs.q: The mineral required in the formation of chlorophyll is:
mcqs.why: Magnesium is an essential part of the chlorophyll molecule; without it leaves turn yellow and photosynthesis suffers.

mcqs.q: The correct word equation for photosynthesis is:
mcqs.why: In the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, carbon dioxide and water are converted into glucose and oxygen; the first option is the equation of respiration.

mcqs.q: The gas released as a by-product of photosynthesis is:
mcqs.why: Oxygen produced in photosynthesis is released through the stomata; animals depend on this oxygen for respiration.

mcqs.q: The broad and flat shape of the leaf helps photosynthesis because it:
options: gives a large surface to absorb maximum sunlight
mcqs.why: A broad, flat and thin leaf exposes a large area to sunlight and lets gases diffuse quickly to the mesophyll cells.

mcqs.q: In the Hydrilla experiment, the gas collected in the test tube is proved to be oxygen because it:
mcqs.why: A glowing splint relights in the collected gas, which is the standard test for oxygen; lime water turning milky is the test for carbon dioxide.

mcqs.q: Plants need nitrogen (nitrates) mainly to make:
options: proteins for growth and new cells
mcqs.why: Nitrogen is used to build proteins, which are required for growth and for making new cells and enzymes in the plant.

mcqs.q: Photosynthesis takes place in:
options: the nucleus of the leaf cells
mcqs.why: Only cells containing chloroplasts (with chlorophyll) can photosynthesise, and only when light is available.

lessons.title: Respiration in Plants
lessons.notes_html:
What is Respiration?

Respiration is the breakdown of glucose with oxygen inside the cells to release energy, producing carbon dioxide and water. It goes on day and night in all living cells.

Word equation: Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy.

Photosynthesis and Respiration Compared

Photosynthesis builds up glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy and releases oxygen; it occurs only in green cells, only in light, and stores energy. Respiration breaks down glucose with oxygen, releases the stored energy, and produces carbon dioxide and water; it occurs in all living cells, day and night. The two processes are opposite and balance each other.

Respiration at Night

At night photosynthesis stops but respiration continues, so the plant takes in oxygen from the air through the stomata of leaves and the pores (lenticels) of stems. This is why we should not sleep under a tree at night: the tree takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide, so the air under it contains more carbon dioxide and less oxygen. During the day, photosynthesis in the same tree takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen, and it also provides the food and oxygen on which almost all animals depend.

Key Points

  • Respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy, in all living cells, day and night.
  • Photosynthesis stores energy and releases oxygen; respiration releases energy and uses oxygen.
  • At night plants absorb oxygen from the air for respiration through stomata and lenticels.

mcqs.q: The products of respiration are carbon dioxide and:
mcqs.why: Respiration breaks down glucose with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water, releasing the energy stored in the food.

mcqs.q: The correct word equation for respiration is:
options: Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy
mcqs.why: In respiration, glucose is oxidised to carbon dioxide and water and the stored energy is released for life activities.

mcqs.q: Respiration takes place:
options: in all living cells, day and night
mcqs.why: Every living cell needs energy continuously, so respiration never stops; photosynthesis, by contrast, needs light and chlorophyll.

mcqs.q: At night, plants obtain oxygen for respiration:
options: from the air through stomata and lenticels
mcqs.why: When photosynthesis stops at night, plants absorb oxygen from the surrounding air through stomata and stem pores (lenticels).

mcqs.q: We should not sleep under a tree at night because at night the tree:
options: takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide
mcqs.why: At night only respiration continues in the tree, so the air beneath it becomes richer in carbon dioxide and poorer in oxygen, which is unhealthy to breathe for long.

mcqs.q: The process that stores energy in glucose is:
mcqs.why: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose; respiration later releases that stored energy.

mcqs.q: Respiration is important for the plant because it:
options: releases the energy stored in food for life activities
mcqs.why: The energy released by respiration is used for growth, absorption of minerals, making new substances and all other life processes.

mcqs.q: Photosynthesis occurs only in:
options: green cells in the presence of light
mcqs.why: Photosynthesis needs chlorophyll (found in green cells) and light energy, so it happens only in green parts during the day.

mcqs.q: Animals benefit from photosynthesis because it provides them with:
mcqs.why: Almost all animal food comes directly or indirectly from plant photosynthesis, and the oxygen animals breathe is released by it.

mcqs.q: Photosynthesis and respiration are opposite processes because photosynthesis:
options: uses carbon dioxide and releases oxygen, while respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide
mcqs.why: The two processes exchange the same gases in opposite directions and balance each other in nature.

chapters.title: Unit 2: Human Respiratory and Circulatory Systems

lessons.title: The Respiratory System and Breathing
lessons.notes_html:
Parts of the Breathing System

The parts involved in breathing are: nose (nostrils), nasal passage, pharynx, larynx, trachea (windpipe), bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and the lungs, assisted by the ribs, intercostal muscles and the diaphragm. The trachea divides into two bronchi, one entering each lung, where they branch into bronchioles ending in tiny air sacs, the alveoli.

Exchange of Gases

Exchange of gases takes place in the alveoli. Their thin walls are surrounded by blood capillaries; oxygen from the inhaled air diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out. Blood is thus oxygenated in the lungs, and the pulmonary vein carries the oxygenated blood to the left atrium of the heart.

How Breathing Works

During inhalation, the intercostal muscles between the ribs contract, lifting the ribs up and out, and the diaphragm flattens; the chest cavity enlarges, pressure inside falls, and air rushes into the lungs. During exhalation these muscles relax, the ribs move down and in, the diaphragm becomes dome-shaped, the chest cavity becomes smaller and air is pushed out.

Breathing and Respiration

Breathing is the physical process of taking air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is the chemical process inside cells in which glucose is broken down with oxygen to release energy. Breathing supplies the oxygen for respiration and removes its carbon dioxide.

Key Points

  • The trachea divides into two bronchi; gases are exchanged in the alveoli.
  • Inhalation: ribs rise, diaphragm flattens, chest expands and air enters.
  • Breathing is physical; respiration is the chemical release of energy in cells.

mcqs.q: Exchange of gases takes place in the:
mcqs.why: The alveoli are tiny thin-walled air sacs wrapped in capillaries, where oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.

mcqs.q: The trachea divides into two:
mcqs.why: The trachea (windpipe) splits into two bronchi, one going to each lung, where they branch further into bronchioles.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a part of the breathing system?
mcqs.why: The oesophagus is the food pipe of the digestive system; the breathing system consists of the nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and lungs.

mcqs.q: During inhalation, the diaphragm:
mcqs.why: When the diaphragm flattens and the ribs lift up and out, the chest cavity enlarges, pressure falls and air rushes into the lungs.

mcqs.q: The tiny air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles are called:
mcqs.why: Bronchioles end in clusters of alveoli, the air sacs where the actual exchange of gases between air and blood occurs.

mcqs.q: Breathing is best defined as:
options: the physical process of taking air in and out of the lungs
the breakdown of glucose in cells
the transport of oxygen by blood
the production of energy in mitochondria
mcqs.why: Breathing (inhalation and exhalation) is a physical process; respiration is the chemical process inside cells that releases energy from glucose.

mcqs.q: During inhalation, the intercostal muscles make the ribs:
mcqs.why: Contraction of the intercostal muscles lifts the ribs up and out, enlarging the chest cavity so that air is drawn in.

mcqs.q: The windpipe is the common name of the:
mcqs.why: The trachea is called the windpipe; it carries air from the larynx down to the two bronchi entering the lungs.

mcqs.q: During exhalation, the chest cavity:
options: becomes larger and air rushes in
becomes smaller and air is pushed out
mcqs.why: In exhalation the ribs move down and in and the diaphragm becomes dome-shaped, shrinking the chest cavity and forcing air out.

mcqs.q: Blood is oxygenated in the:
mcqs.why: In the alveoli of the lungs, oxygen diffuses into the blood capillaries and carbon dioxide leaves; the oxygenated blood then goes to the left atrium.

lessons.title: Respiration: Aerobic and Anaerobic
lessons.notes_html:
Aerobic Respiration

Aerobic respiration breaks down glucose completely in the presence of oxygen, producing carbon dioxide, water and a large amount of energy. It takes place in the mitochondria of the cells.

Anaerobic Respiration

Anaerobic respiration takes place without oxygen; glucose is broken down incompletely, releasing much less energy. In yeast the products are ethanol and carbon dioxide. In our muscles, during hard exercise when oxygen supply is insufficient, the products are lactic acid and energy; the build-up of lactic acid causes cramps and tiredness, and during rest extra oxygen breaks it down — which is why we breathe heavily after exercise.

Burning and Respiration

Burning is a fast, uncontrolled chemical reaction outside the body in which fuel combines with oxygen at high temperature, releasing energy suddenly as heat and light. Respiration is a slow, controlled, step-by-step breakdown of glucose inside living cells at body temperature, releasing energy gradually in a usable form without flame.

Role of the Circulatory System

Cellular respiration needs glucose and oxygen and produces carbon dioxide. The circulatory system delivers oxygen from the lungs and glucose from the digestive system to every cell, and carries the carbon dioxide away to the lungs for removal. Oxygen is the gas used in respiration; carbon dioxide is the waste gas removed in exhalation.

Key Points

  • Aerobic respiration (in mitochondria) releases much more energy than anaerobic respiration.
  • Anaerobic products: ethanol + carbon dioxide in yeast; lactic acid in muscles.
  • Respiration is slow and controlled; burning is fast and uncontrolled.

mcqs.q: Aerobic respiration takes place in the:
mcqs.why: Aerobic respiration, the complete breakdown of glucose with oxygen, occurs in the mitochondria, the energy-releasing organelles of the cell.

mcqs.q: The products of anaerobic respiration in yeast are ________ along with energy:
mcqs.why: Yeast respires anaerobically (fermentation) to produce ethanol and carbon dioxide; muscles instead produce lactic acid.

mcqs.q: Anaerobic respiration in human muscles produces:
mcqs.why: When oxygen is short during hard exercise, muscle cells break glucose into lactic acid and energy; the lactic acid build-up causes cramps.

mcqs.q: Muscle cramps during vigorous exercise are caused by the build-up of:
mcqs.why: Anaerobic respiration in the muscles produces lactic acid, whose accumulation causes cramps and fatigue until extra oxygen breaks it down during rest.

mcqs.q: Compared with anaerobic respiration, aerobic respiration releases:
mcqs.why: Aerobic respiration breaks glucose down completely to carbon dioxide and water, releasing far more energy than the incomplete anaerobic breakdown.

mcqs.q: Burning differs from respiration because burning is:
options: fast and uncontrolled, releasing energy suddenly as heat and light
mcqs.why: Burning is a rapid, uncontrolled reaction at high temperature outside the body, while respiration releases energy slowly and gradually inside cells.

mcqs.q: The circulatory system supports cellular respiration by:
options: delivering oxygen and glucose to the cells and carrying away carbon dioxide
mcqs.why: Blood transports oxygen from the lungs and glucose from the digestive system to every cell, and removes the carbon dioxide produced in respiration.

mcqs.q: Anaerobic respiration in muscles takes place when:
options: oxygen supply cannot keep up with the energy demand of hard exercise
mcqs.why: During sprinting and other vigorous exercise, muscles need energy faster than blood can supply oxygen, so they respire anaerobically for a while.

mcqs.q: After hard exercise we keep breathing heavily for some time because:
options: extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid formed in the muscles
mcqs.why: The heavy breathing repays the oxygen debt: the extra oxygen oxidises the accumulated lactic acid in the muscles.

mcqs.q: The complete breakdown of glucose in aerobic respiration produces:
options: carbon dioxide, water and a large amount of energy
ethanol, carbon dioxide and little energy
mcqs.why: Aerobic respiration fully oxidises glucose to carbon dioxide and water, releasing the maximum energy stored in the glucose.

lessons.title: The Heart, Blood Vessels and Blood
lessons.notes_html:
The Heart and Its Working

The human heart has four chambers: the right atrium and right ventricle, and the left atrium and left ventricle. The atria receive blood and the ventricles pump it out. Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium, passes into the right ventricle and is pumped through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns by the pulmonary vein to the left atrium, passes into the left ventricle and is pumped through the aorta to the whole body — a double circulation repeated about 70–72 times a minute at rest. Valves (tricuspid on the right, bicuspid/mitral on the left, and semilunar valves at the aorta and pulmonary artery) make blood flow in one direction only and prevent backflow.

Blood Vessels

Arteries carry blood away from the heart; they have thick, muscular, elastic walls, carry blood under high pressure and have no valves. Veins carry blood towards the heart; they have thinner walls, a wider lumen, low pressure and valves to stop backflow. Capillaries are microscopic vessels with walls one cell thick joining arteries to veins; through their walls food, gases and wastes are exchanged between blood and tissues. Capillaries exchange materials with tissues, while alveoli exchange gases with air — both have very thin walls.

Composition of Blood

Blood consists of plasma (about 55%) and blood cells (about 45%). Plasma is a pale yellow liquid, mostly water, carrying dissolved food, hormones, salts and wastes. Red blood cells contain haemoglobin and carry oxygen; white blood cells fight germs and produce antibodies; platelets help in clotting of blood at wounds.

Key Points

  • The heart has four chambers; the left side handles oxygenated blood, the right side deoxygenated blood.
  • Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins return it; capillaries exchange materials with tissues.
  • Plasma is about 55% of blood; platelets help in clotting.

mcqs.q: The part of the heart which receives blood from the lungs is the:
mcqs.why: Oxygenated blood from the lungs returns through the pulmonary vein into the left atrium, then passes to the left ventricle.

mcqs.q: The left atrium opens into the:
mcqs.why: Blood received by the left atrium passes through the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the left ventricle, which pumps it into the aorta.

mcqs.q: The right atrium receives:
mcqs.why: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the whole body and passes it to the right ventricle, which sends it to the lungs.

mcqs.q: Blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart are:
mcqs.why: Arteries have thick muscular walls to bear high pressure and carry blood away from the heart to the organs.

mcqs.q: Exchange of material between the body tissues and blood takes place in the:
mcqs.why: Capillaries have walls only one cell thick, so food, gases and wastes can pass between the blood and the body tissues.

mcqs.q: Which of the following plays an important role in blood clotting?
mcqs.why: Platelets help the blood to clot at a wound, sealing it so that blood loss stops and germs cannot enter.

mcqs.q: The number of chambers in the human heart is:
mcqs.why: The heart has two atria and two ventricles — four chambers in all — which keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate.

mcqs.q: The valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle is the:
mcqs.why: The bicuspid or mitral valve guards the opening from the left atrium to the left ventricle; the tricuspid valve is on the right side.

mcqs.q: Plasma makes up about what percentage of the blood?
mcqs.why: Blood is about 55% plasma (the pale yellow liquid part) and about 45% blood cells suspended in it.

mcqs.q: Red blood cells carry oxygen with the help of:
mcqs.why: Red blood cells contain the red pigment haemoglobin, which picks up oxygen in the lungs and releases it to the body cells.

lessons.title: Pathogens and Infectious Diseases
lessons.notes_html:
Pathogens

A pathogen is a micro-organism that causes disease in the body, such as a virus, bacterium, fungus or parasite. Infection is the entry, growth and multiplication of pathogens inside the body; it may damage tissues and produce the symptoms of a disease. Viruses are the smallest pathogens; they are not complete cells and multiply only inside living cells, causing diseases like COVID-19, flu and hepatitis. Bacteria are single-celled organisms; many are harmless but some cause typhoid and tuberculosis. Fungi are plant-like organisms that grow on skin and food, causing diseases like ringworm. Note that a bacterial cell has no nuclear membrane.

How Pathogens Enter the Body

Pathogens enter the body through the nose and mouth with air, food and water, through cuts in the skin, and by insect bites and contact with infected persons.

Infectious Diseases and Their Transmission

Infectious diseases are diseases caused by pathogens which can spread from an infected person (or animal) to a healthy person. Examples are COVID-19, typhoid, hepatitis (inflammation of the liver), dengue, tuberculosis and influenza. Diseases spread by direct contact, through the air in droplets from coughs and sneezes, through contaminated water and food, through the bite of insects such as mosquitoes (dengue, malaria), and through infected blood and unsterilised needles. Knowing the mode of transmission helps us block it.

Key Points

  • A pathogen is a disease-causing micro-organism; infection is its growth inside the body.
  • Viruses multiply only inside living cells; bacteria are single-celled; fungi grow on skin and food.
  • Infectious diseases spread through air, water, food, contact, insects and infected blood.

mcqs.q: ________ is the inflammation of the liver:
mcqs.why: Hepatitis is the inflammation of the liver, usually caused by viruses; tuberculosis affects the lungs and typhoid the intestines.

mcqs.q: A pathogen is:
options: a type of white blood cell
a vitamin needed by the body
mcqs.why: Pathogens are disease-causing micro-organisms such as viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites that disturb the normal working of the body.

mcqs.q: Infection means:
options: the entry, growth and multiplication of pathogens inside the body
mcqs.why: When pathogens enter the body and multiply, the resulting infection may damage tissues and produce disease symptoms.

mcqs.q: Which pathogens are not complete cells and multiply only inside living cells?
mcqs.why: Viruses are the smallest pathogens; they lack a complete cell structure and can multiply only inside the living cells of a host.

mcqs.q: A nuclear membrane is NOT found in a:
mcqs.why: Bacterial cells have no true nucleus and no nuclear membrane; their genetic material lies free in the cytoplasm, unlike plant, animal and fungal cells.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an infectious disease?
mcqs.why: Typhoid is caused by bacteria and spreads through contaminated water and food; diabetes, rickets and anaemia are not caused by pathogens.

mcqs.q: Dengue and malaria are spread from person to person by:
mcqs.why: These diseases are transmitted by insect vectors: the pathogens are carried in the bite of infected mosquitoes.

mcqs.q: Ringworm is a disease caused by:
mcqs.why: Ringworm is a fungal infection of the skin; fungi are plant-like organisms that grow on skin and food.

mcqs.q: Pathogens can enter the body through:
options: the nose and mouth with air, food and water
mcqs.why: The main entry routes are the nose and mouth (air, food, water), cuts in the skin, insect bites and contact with infected persons.

mcqs.q: Diseases spread through the air mainly by:
options: droplets from coughs and sneezes of an infected person
mcqs.why: Coughing and sneezing spray tiny droplets containing pathogens into the air, which healthy people then inhale — the route for COVID-19 and influenza.

lessons.title: Barriers and Non-specific Defence
lessons.notes_html:
Physical Barriers

The skin is the main physical barrier: its outer layer stops germs entering, and the pigment melanin protects against the harmful effects of sunlight. Hairs in the nose trap dust and germs, and mucus in the air passages traps pathogens which are swept out. Tears wash the eyes and contain lysozyme, saliva also contains germ-killing substances, and the hydrochloric acid in gastric juice kills many germs swallowed with food. Blood clotting seals wounds so germs cannot enter.

Non-specific Defence

Non-specific defence attacks all pathogens in the same general way. If germs cross the barriers, the injured area becomes inflamed — red, warm and swollen — and phagocytes reach there and engulf the germs. This eating of pathogens by white blood cells is called phagocytosis: the phagocyte surrounds the germ with its cell membrane, takes it in and destroys it with enzymes. Fever raises body temperature, which slows the growth of many pathogens, and substances like lysozyme and stomach acid destroy germs chemically.

Key Points

  • Skin (with melanin), nose hairs, mucus, tears, saliva and stomach acid are the body's barriers.
  • Phagocytosis is the engulfing and digestion of germs by phagocyte white blood cells.
  • Inflammation and fever are non-specific defences against all pathogens.

mcqs.q: The pigment in the skin that protects from the harmful effects of sunlight is:
mcqs.why: Melanin is the skin pigment that absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays of sunlight and protects the deeper tissues.

mcqs.q: Hydrochloric acid is found in:
mcqs.why: The hydrochloric acid in gastric juice of the stomach kills many germs swallowed with food, forming a chemical barrier.

mcqs.q: Phagocytosis is:
options: the engulfing and digestion of pathogens by white blood cells
mcqs.why: In phagocytosis a phagocyte surrounds a germ with its membrane, takes it in and destroys it with enzymes.

mcqs.q: The main physical barrier of the body against germs is the:
mcqs.why: The outer layer of the skin stops germs from entering the body; it is the first and main physical barrier.

mcqs.q: Tears protect the eyes because they contain:
mcqs.why: Tears wash the eyes and contain the enzyme lysozyme, which destroys many bacteria; lysozyme is also present in saliva.

mcqs.q: When germs enter a tissue, the area becomes red, warm and swollen. This response is called:
mcqs.why: Inflammation is a non-specific defence: blood flow to the injured area increases and phagocytes arrive to engulf the germs.

mcqs.q: Fever helps the body fight pathogens because the higher temperature:
options: slows the growth of many pathogens
mcqs.why: Many pathogens grow best at normal body temperature; the raised temperature of fever makes conditions unfavourable for them.

mcqs.q: Hairs in the nose and mucus in the air passages defend the body by:
options: trapping dust and germs entering with air
mcqs.why: Nose hairs and sticky mucus trap inhaled dust and pathogens, which are then swept out before reaching the lungs.

mcqs.q: Blood clotting defends the body by:
options: sealing wounds so germs cannot enter
mcqs.why: A clot plugs a cut in the skin, stopping blood loss and closing the entry route for pathogens.

mcqs.q: Non-specific defence is called 'non-specific' because it:
options: is produced in the bone marrow only
attacks all pathogens in the same general way
mcqs.why: Barriers, inflammation, fever and phagocytosis act against every kind of pathogen in the same way, unlike the specific antibody response.

lessons.title: The Immune System and Staying Healthy
lessons.notes_html:
Antigens and Antibodies

An antigen is a substance, usually a protein on the surface of a pathogen, that the immune system recognises as foreign. Its presence triggers the body to produce specific antibodies against it — proteins that destroy that particular pathogen.

Parts of the Immune System

The immune system includes the bone marrow, where billions of new blood cells are produced daily; white blood cells (lymphocytes and phagocytes) which fight germs; antibodies; and the lymphoid organs — the spleen, thymus, tonsils and lymph nodes — where lymphocytes are stored and activated. The thymus matures T-lymphocytes, the spleen filters blood, the tonsils trap germs entering through the mouth and nose, and lymph nodes filter lymph.

Avoiding Infections and Strengthening Immunity

We can avoid infections by washing hands with soap, drinking clean water, eating properly cooked and covered food, and keeping our surroundings clean. Wearing masks in crowds, covering the mouth while coughing, keeping distance from sick persons and getting vaccinated in time also protect us. Personal hygiene — bathing daily, washing hands before eating and after using the toilet, brushing teeth twice a day, keeping nails trimmed and wearing clean clothes — stops germs spreading. Immunity is strengthened by a balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, proteins and vitamins, regular exercise, sufficient sleep, and avoiding smoking and stress.

Key Points

  • An antigen is the foreign substance on a pathogen that triggers antibody production.
  • Bone marrow makes new blood cells daily; lymphoid organs store and activate lymphocytes.
  • Hygiene, clean food and water, and vaccination prevent infections.

mcqs.q: Billions of new blood cells are produced daily in the:
mcqs.why: The bone marrow is the factory of the blood: billions of new red and white blood cells are produced there every day.

mcqs.q: An antigen is:
options: a substance on a pathogen that triggers the production of antibodies
mcqs.why: Antigens are usually proteins on the surface of a pathogen; when the immune system recognises them as foreign, it produces specific antibodies.

mcqs.q: Antibodies are:
mcqs.why: Antibodies are proteins produced by lymphocytes, each shaped to attack one particular kind of pathogen.

mcqs.q: Which organ filters the blood and stores lymphocytes?
mcqs.why: The spleen is a lymphoid organ that filters blood, removes worn-out cells and stores lymphocytes; the thymus matures T-lymphocytes.

mcqs.q: The lymphoid organ that matures T-lymphocytes is the:
mcqs.why: Lymphocytes produced in the bone marrow mature into T-lymphocytes in the thymus, an organ of the immune system.

mcqs.q: Which habit best prevents the spread of germs through hands?
options: washing hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet
mcqs.why: Hand washing with soap removes pathogens picked up from surfaces and the toilet before they can enter through the mouth.

mcqs.q: Vaccination protects us because it:
options: trains the immune system to produce antibodies against a disease before we catch it
mcqs.why: A vaccine presents a harmless form of the pathogen's antigen, so the body prepares antibodies and can fight the real disease quickly.

mcqs.q: Personal hygiene includes:
options: bathing daily, brushing teeth twice a day and keeping nails trimmed
mcqs.why: Keeping the body and clothes clean — bathing, brushing, trimmed nails, clean clothes — removes germs and stops them spreading.

mcqs.q: Our immune system becomes stronger when we:
options: eat a balanced diet, exercise regularly and sleep enough
mcqs.why: Fruits, vegetables, proteins and vitamins, regular exercise and sufficient sleep keep the immune system strong; smoking and stress weaken it.

mcqs.q: Tonsils help the immune system by:
options: trapping germs entering through the mouth and nose
mcqs.why: The tonsils are lymphoid organs placed at the entrance of the throat, where they trap and fight germs entering with air and food.

lessons.title: Inside the Atom
lessons.notes_html:
The Atom

An atom is the smallest particle of an element that keeps the properties of that element and takes part in chemical reactions. An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atoms, all having the same atomic number; it cannot be broken into simpler substances by chemical means. Examples are hydrogen, oxygen, carbon and iron; 118 elements are known.

Parts of the Atom

The central part of the atom is the nucleus, which contains protons (positive charge) and neutrons (no charge — neutral). Electrons, the particles with a negative charge, revolve around the nucleus in shells. The mass of the atom is almost entirely due to the nucleus, because protons and neutrons are heavy while electrons have negligible mass.

Key Points

  • Atom = nucleus (protons + neutrons) with electrons revolving in shells.
  • Protons are positive, electrons negative, neutrons neutral.
  • Almost all the mass of an atom is in its nucleus.

mcqs.q: The central part of an atom is called the:
mcqs.why: The nucleus is the dense central part of the atom containing protons and neutrons; electrons revolve around it in shells.

mcqs.q: The particle of an atom having a negative charge on it is the:
mcqs.why: Electrons carry a negative charge; protons are positive and neutrons carry no charge at all.

mcqs.q: The mass of an atom is almost due to the:
mcqs.why: Protons and neutrons in the nucleus carry almost the whole mass of the atom, while the mass of electrons is negligible.

mcqs.q: What type of charge is present on a neutron?
mcqs.why: The neutron is a neutral particle present in the nucleus; its mass is almost equal to that of a proton but it has no electric charge.

mcqs.q: An atom is:
options: the smallest particle of an element that keeps its properties
mcqs.why: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that retains the element's properties and takes part in chemical reactions.

mcqs.q: An element is a pure substance made of:
options: only one kind of atoms, all with the same atomic number
mcqs.why: All atoms of an element have the same atomic number; an element cannot be broken into simpler substances by chemical means.

mcqs.q: Protons and neutrons are found in the:
mcqs.why: The nucleus at the centre of the atom contains the protons and neutrons; electrons move around it in shells.

mcqs.q: Which particle has almost the same mass as a proton but no charge?
mcqs.why: The neutron's mass is almost equal to the proton's, but unlike the proton it carries no charge.

mcqs.q: How many elements are known in total?
mcqs.why: 118 elements are known, each made of one kind of atom and arranged in the Periodic Table in order of atomic number.

mcqs.q: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in:
mcqs.why: Electrons are arranged in shells or energy levels around the nucleus, each shell holding a maximum number fixed by the 2n2 rule.

lessons.title: Atomic Number, Mass Number and Isotopes
lessons.notes_html:
Atomic Number and Mass Number

The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons present in the nucleus of an atom. It is also equal to the number of electrons in a neutral atom, and it identifies the element; elements in the Periodic Table are arranged in increasing atomic number. An element with fifteen protons therefore has atomic number 15. The mass number (A) is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus: A = protons + neutrons.

Reading a Nuclear Symbol

The symbol 13Al27 (aluminium) shows atomic number 13 as subscript and mass number 27 as superscript. So an aluminium atom has 13 protons, 13 electrons and 27 − 13 = 14 neutrons.

Isotopes

Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number (same protons) but different mass numbers because they contain different numbers of neutrons — for example hydrogen, deuterium and tritium. Isotopes have important uses: carbon-14 finds the age of old fossils and objects (radiocarbon dating); iodine-131 treats thyroid diseases; cobalt-60 is used in radiotherapy for cancer and to sterilise medical equipment; uranium-235 is fuel in nuclear reactors; and tracer isotopes are used in agriculture and medicine.

Key Points

  • Atomic number Z = number of protons; mass number A = protons + neutrons.
  • Neutrons = A − Z (aluminium-27 has 14 neutrons).
  • Isotopes differ in neutrons and mass number, not in atomic number.

mcqs.q: An element with fifteen protons in its atomic nucleus has atomic number:
mcqs.why: Atomic number is simply the number of protons in the nucleus, so an atom with fifteen protons has atomic number 15.

mcqs.q: The particles of an element having different mass numbers are called:
mcqs.why: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, hence different mass numbers.

mcqs.q: The mass number of an atom is:
options: the number of protons plus the number of neutrons
the number of protons minus neutrons
mcqs.why: Mass number A = protons + neutrons, since these two heavy particles make up almost the whole mass of the atom.

mcqs.q: The symbol 13Al27 shows that an aluminium atom has:
mcqs.why: Atomic number 13 gives 13 protons (and 13 electrons); neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 27 − 13 = 14.

mcqs.q: Isotopes of an element have the same:
mcqs.why: Isotopes are the same element, so their proton number (atomic number) is identical; only the neutron number and mass number differ.

mcqs.q: An atom has 11 protons and 12 neutrons. Its mass number is:
mcqs.why: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 11 + 12 = 23. This is sodium, whose atomic number is 11.

mcqs.q: Carbon-14 is used to:
options: find the age of old fossils and objects
mcqs.why: Radiocarbon dating with carbon-14 measures the age of once-living material; iodine-131 treats the thyroid and uranium-235 fuels reactors.

mcqs.q: The isotope used as fuel in nuclear reactors is:
mcqs.why: Uranium-235 undergoes fission in nuclear reactors to release energy; cobalt-60 is used in radiotherapy and sterilisation.

mcqs.q: In a neutral atom, the atomic number is also equal to the number of:
mcqs.why: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so atomic number = protons = electrons.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen, deuterium and tritium are isotopes because they have:
options: the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
mcqs.why: All three have one proton (atomic number 1) but zero, one and two neutrons respectively, giving mass numbers 1, 2 and 3.

lessons.title: Electron Shells and the Periodic Table
lessons.notes_html:
Shells and Their Capacity

Electrons are arranged in shells around the nucleus, named K, L, M, N for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th shells. The maximum number of electrons in a shell is given by the formula 2n2, where n is the shell number: K (n=1) holds 2, L (n=2) holds 8, M (n=3) holds 18 and N (n=4) holds 32. The arrangement of electrons in shells is the electronic configuration; for example sodium (11) is 2, 8, 1 and chlorine (17) is 2, 8, 7.

Some Elements and Their Configurations

Oxygen (atomic number 8) is in group 16 and period 2; its configuration 2,6 means it needs 2 more electrons to complete its valence shell. Sodium (symbol Na, atomic number 11) is in period 3 and group 1 — the family of alkali metals. Magnesium (12) is 2, 8, 2; argon (18) is 2, 8, 8, a complete outer shell, hence a noble gas. Hydrogen is the element whose period number and group number are the same (period 1, group 1).

The Periodic Table and Families

The Periodic Table has seven periods (horizontal rows) and 18 groups (vertical columns). Families: alkali metals (group 1): lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium, francium; alkaline earth metals (group 2): beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium, radium; halogens (group 17): fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine; noble gases (group 18): helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon. Helium (2) and neon (2,8) have completely filled valence shells, so they are stable and exist as single-atom molecules.

Key Points

  • Shell capacity follows 2n2: K=2, L=8, M=18, N=32.
  • Electronic configuration shows the distribution of electrons in shells, e.g. chlorine 2, 8, 7.
  • The Periodic Table has 7 periods; group 1 = alkali metals, group 17 = halogens, group 18 = noble gases.

mcqs.q: The letter K is used to express the ________ shell around the nucleus of an atom:
mcqs.why: The shells are named K, L, M, N starting from the nucleus, so K is the 1st (innermost) shell and holds at most 2 electrons.

mcqs.q: The total number of electrons which the M shell can accommodate is:
mcqs.why: By the 2n2 rule with n=3 for the M shell: 2 × 3 × 3 = 18 electrons at most.

mcqs.q: The formula showing the maximum number of electrons in a shell is:
mcqs.why: Maximum electrons in shell number n is 2n2: for n=1 it gives 2 (K shell), for n=2 it gives 8 (L shell), and so on.

mcqs.q: How many periods are there in the Periodic Table?
mcqs.why: The Periodic Table has seven horizontal rows called periods and eighteen vertical columns called groups.

mcqs.q: The atomic number of the element present in period 2 and group 15 of the Periodic Table is:
mcqs.why: Period 2 runs from lithium (3) to neon (10); counting to group 15 in that period gives nitrogen, whose atomic number is 7.

mcqs.q: Electronic configuration means:
options: the number of protons in the nucleus
the total mass of the atom
the arrangement of electrons of an atom in its shells around the nucleus
mcqs.why: Electronic configuration describes how electrons are distributed among the shells, e.g. sodium is 2, 8, 1 and chlorine is 2, 8, 7.

mcqs.q: The electronic configuration of chlorine (atomic number 17) is:
mcqs.why: The K shell takes 2, the L shell takes 8, and the remaining 17 − 10 = 7 electrons go into the M shell: 2, 8, 7.

mcqs.q: Oxygen (atomic number 8, configuration 2,6) requires how many electrons to complete its valence shell?
mcqs.why: Oxygen has 6 electrons in its outer shell; it needs 2 more to reach the stable octet of 8.

mcqs.q: Sodium belongs to the family of:
mcqs.why: Sodium is in group 1 of the Periodic Table, the highly reactive family called the alkali metals.

mcqs.q: Helium and neon exist as single-atom (monatomic) molecules because:
options: they have completely filled valence shells and are stable
mcqs.why: Helium (2) and neon (2,8) already have complete outer shells, so they are stable and unreactive — the noble gases.

lessons.title: Physical and Chemical Changes
lessons.notes_html:
Physical Change

A physical change is a change in which no new substance is formed and the composition of the substance stays the same; only its state, shape or size changes. It is usually temporary and reversible. Examples: melting of ice into water and freezing it back, boiling of water into steam, dissolving salt in water, cutting of paper and breaking of glass. Freezing of a liquid and heating a solution of common salt are physical changes.

Chemical Change

A chemical change is a change in which one or more new substances with different properties are formed by a change in composition. It is usually permanent and difficult to reverse. During a chemical change the composition and properties of the substances are changed and new substances are formed. Examples: burning of wood, rusting of iron, and sugar heated strongly until it chars.

Changes of State are Physical

When water changes between ice, liquid and steam, no new substance is formed — water remains water in all three states. Melting (fusion), boiling (vaporisation), condensation and freezing (solidification) are all physical changes. Drying of wet clothes is also physical: the water evaporates into vapour, helped by the sun's heat, wind and the spread-out surface of the clothes.

Key Points

  • Physical change: no new substance, composition unchanged, usually reversible.
  • Chemical change: new substances with different properties are formed; usually permanent.
  • All changes of state (melting, boiling, condensation, freezing) are physical changes.

mcqs.q: A physical change occurs when:
options: a solution of common salt is heated
mcqs.why: Heating a salt solution only evaporates the water — no new substance is formed. Rusting, burning and strong heating of sugar all form new substances.

mcqs.q: Which of the following happens during a chemical change?
options: Composition of the substances is changed
The substance can always be recovered unchanged
mcqs.why: In a chemical change the composition changes and new substances with different properties are formed; the change is usually permanent.

mcqs.q: Freezing of a liquid is a:
mcqs.why: Freezing only changes the state of the substance; its composition stays the same and the change can be reversed by melting.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a chemical change?
mcqs.why: Burning wood forms new substances (ash, carbon dioxide, water vapour) and cannot be reversed; the others change only state or form.

mcqs.q: A physical change is usually:
mcqs.why: Since no new substance is formed in a physical change, the original substance can usually be recovered, e.g. water from ice or salt from its solution.

mcqs.q: When wet clothes dry in the sun, the water:
options: changes into water vapour by evaporation — a physical change
mcqs.why: The sun's heat gives water molecules the energy to escape as vapour; the water itself is unchanged, so drying is a physical change.

mcqs.q: In the changes of state of water (ice → water → steam), the chemical changes are:
mcqs.why: Water remains water in the solid, liquid and gaseous states; melting, boiling, condensation and freezing form no new substance.

mcqs.q: Dissolving common salt in water is a physical change because:
options: the salt's composition stays the same and it can be recovered by evaporation
mcqs.why: The dissolved salt is chemically unchanged; evaporating the water gives the salt back, showing the change is physical and reversible.

mcqs.q: Which process is a chemical change?
options: strong heating of sugar until it turns black
mcqs.why: Strongly heated sugar decomposes into new substances (carbon and water vapour); condensation, breaking and boiling change only state or form.

mcqs.q: During a chemical change, the new substances formed have:
options: the same properties as the original substances
different properties from the original substances
mcqs.why: A chemical change produces substances whose properties — colour, state, reactivity — are different from those of the starting substances.

lessons.title: Physical and Chemical Properties
lessons.notes_html:
Physical Properties

A physical property is a property of a substance that can be observed or measured without changing its composition, e.g. colour, hardness, density, melting point, boiling point, solubility and conductance. Materials are chosen for uses according to their physical properties: copper and aluminium for electric wires because they conduct electricity; wood and plastic for handles because they are insulators; metals for utensils because they conduct heat and are hard and strong; glass for windows because it is transparent; rubber for tyres because it is flexible and waterproof.

Chemical Properties

A chemical property describes how a substance reacts and changes into new substances, e.g. flammability, oxidation (rusting, tarnishing) and reaction with acids. It can only be observed during a chemical change. Chemical properties also decide uses: fuels like petrol, gas and coal are used because they burn and release energy; gold and platinum are used for jewellery because they do not react or tarnish easily; sodium is stored under kerosene because it is very reactive; stainless steel is preferred where ordinary iron would rust.

The Odd One Out

Solubility, conductance and boiling of a substance are all physical properties (no composition change), while oxidation is a chemical property — that is why oxidation is the one different from the other three.

Key Points

  • Physical properties are observed without changing composition: colour, density, solubility, conductance, melting and boiling points.
  • Chemical properties appear only in chemical changes: flammability, oxidation, reaction with acids.
  • Both kinds of properties decide the uses of materials.

mcqs.q: Three of the following are alike. Select the one that is different from the others:
mcqs.why: Solubility, conductance and boiling are physical properties involving no change of composition; oxidation is a chemical property shown in a chemical change.

mcqs.q: A physical property of a substance is one that:
options: appears only when the substance burns
changes the substance into a new one
can be observed or measured without changing its composition
mcqs.why: Colour, hardness, density, melting point, boiling point, solubility and conductance are all observed while the substance stays chemically the same.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a chemical property?
mcqs.why: Flammability describes how a substance burns — a reaction forming new substances — so it is a chemical property; the others are physical.

mcqs.q: Copper and aluminium are used for electric wires because of their physical property of:
mcqs.why: Conductance is a physical property; metals conduct electricity, while insulators like wood and plastic are used for handles.

mcqs.q: Glass is used for windows because it is:
mcqs.why: Transparency is a physical property of glass that lets light pass through, making it suitable for windows.

mcqs.q: Gold and platinum are used for jewellery mainly because they:
options: do not react or tarnish easily
mcqs.why: Their chemical unreactivity keeps jewellery bright for years — a use decided by a chemical property, unlike reactive metals that corrode.

mcqs.q: Sodium metal is stored under kerosene because:
options: it is very reactive and would react with air and moisture
mcqs.why: Sodium's high reactivity (a chemical property) makes it react violently with air and water, so it is kept under kerosene for safety.

mcqs.q: Rubber is used for tyres because it is:
mcqs.why: Flexibility and being waterproof are physical properties that make rubber suitable for tyres that grip the road and resist water.

mcqs.q: Which of these can only be observed during a chemical change?
mcqs.why: A chemical property such as reacting with acids is seen only when the substance actually changes into new substances; melting point, boiling point and density are physical measurements.

mcqs.q: Fuels like petrol and coal are useful because of their chemical property of:
mcqs.why: Combustion is a chemical change; fuels are chosen because they burn in oxygen and release large amounts of energy.

lessons.title: Melting, Freezing and Boiling Points
lessons.notes_html:
Melting Point and Freezing Point

The melting point is the fixed temperature at which a solid changes into a liquid at atmospheric pressure, e.g. ice melts at 0°C; at this temperature solid and liquid exist together. The freezing point is the fixed temperature at which a liquid changes into a solid, e.g. water freezes at 0°C. For a pure substance the freezing point is the same as its melting point.

Boiling Point

The boiling point is the fixed temperature at which a liquid boils and its vapour pressure becomes equal to the external (atmospheric) pressure, e.g. water boils at 100°C at sea level.

Solubility

Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that can dissolve in 100 g of a solvent at a particular temperature to form a saturated solution. It generally increases with temperature for solids.

Boiling Points Separate Crude Oil

Crude oil is a mixture of liquids (petrol, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil, bitumen), each with a different boiling point. In fractional distillation the mixture is heated in a fractionating column; vapours rise and condense at the height where the temperature equals their boiling point. Liquids with low boiling points (petrol) rise highest, while those with high boiling points (bitumen) stay near the bottom.

Key Points

  • Ice melts and water freezes at 0°C; water boils at 100°C at sea level.
  • At the boiling point, the liquid's vapour pressure equals the external pressure.
  • Different boiling points make fractional distillation of crude oil possible.

mcqs.q: The temperature at which a liquid's vapour pressure is equal to the external pressure surrounding the liquid is its:
mcqs.why: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure; for water at sea level this happens at 100°C.

mcqs.q: The melting point of ice is:
mcqs.why: Ice melts at the fixed temperature of 0°C, at which solid ice and liquid water exist together.

mcqs.q: For a pure substance, the freezing point is:
options: the same as its melting point
mcqs.why: Melting and freezing are opposite changes at the same fixed temperature; water freezes at 0°C, exactly where ice melts.

mcqs.q: Solubility is defined as the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in:
options: 1 litre of any liquid at any temperature
100 g of solvent at a particular temperature
the whole solvent in the beaker
mcqs.why: Solubility is measured per 100 g of solvent at a stated temperature, giving the amount needed to form a saturated solution.

mcqs.q: The solubility of most solids in water, on heating:
mcqs.why: For most solid solutes, solubility increases with temperature, so hot water can dissolve more of the solid than cold water.

mcqs.q: In fractional distillation of crude oil, the components separate because they have different:
mcqs.why: Each fraction condenses at the height of the column where the temperature equals its own boiling point — petrol highest, bitumen lowest.

mcqs.q: Which fraction of crude oil rises highest in the fractionating column?
mcqs.why: Petrol has one of the lowest boiling points, so its vapours rise highest before condensing; bitumen, with a very high boiling point, stays at the bottom.

mcqs.q: At the melting point of a substance:
mcqs.why: Melting takes place at a fixed temperature at which the solid and liquid forms are present together until melting is complete.

mcqs.q: Water boils at 100°C only when:
options: it is in a closed bottle
it is pure and at sea-level atmospheric pressure
mcqs.why: The boiling point is defined at standard atmospheric pressure; on mountains, where pressure is lower, water boils below 100°C.

mcqs.q: The process by which a liquid changes into a solid at its freezing point is called:
mcqs.why: Freezing (solidification) is the change of a liquid into a solid at the freezing point — one of the physical changes of state.

lessons.title: Oxygen, Combustion, Rusting and Tarnishing
lessons.notes_html:
The Role of Oxygen

Oxygen takes part in many natural chemical reactions: respiration, in which food is oxidised to release energy; combustion of fuels; rusting of iron and tarnishing of silver; and decay of dead bodies and food spoilage. During combustion a substance reacts with oxygen. Heating solid potassium chlorate produces the gas oxygen, and passing electric current through water produces hydrogen and oxygen.

Rusting and Its Prevention

Rusting is the slow chemical reaction of iron with oxygen and moisture of air, forming a reddish-brown film of iron oxide (rust) on its surface, which weakens iron objects. Iron is protected by cutting off contact with air and moisture: painting, applying grease or oil, galvanisation (coating with zinc), electroplating with chromium or tin, and keeping objects dry.

Tarnishing

Tarnishing is the dulling and discolouration of a metal surface due to a chemical reaction with substances in air. Silver reacts with hydrogen sulphide and oxygen to form black silver sulphide: Silver + Hydrogen sulphide + Oxygen → Silver sulphide + Water.

Word Equations

Hydrogen + Oxygen → Water. Carbon + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide. Methane + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water (methane is the kitchen gas; its reactants are methane and oxygen, and heat and light are also produced). Nitrogen + Hydrogen → Ammonia. Iron + Sulphur → Iron sulphide. Emissions from combustion of fuels (carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, smoke) cause air pollution, acid rain, smog and global warming.

Key Points

  • Combustion is reaction with oxygen; oxygen is also needed for respiration, rusting and decay.
  • Rust is iron oxide, formed by iron + oxygen + moisture; painting, greasing and galvanisation prevent it.
  • Tarnishing of silver forms black silver sulphide.

mcqs.q: A gas produced on heating solid potassium chlorate is:
mcqs.why: Heating potassium chlorate decomposes it and releases oxygen gas — a standard laboratory preparation of oxygen.

mcqs.q: What are the products when electric current is passed through water?
mcqs.why: Electrolysis splits water into its two elements, hydrogen and oxygen — the reverse of hydrogen burning in oxygen to form water.

mcqs.q: A piece of iron kept in open air for 5 days forms a film of corrosion which is:
mcqs.why: Iron reacts slowly with oxygen and moisture of the air to form reddish-brown iron oxide, called rust.

mcqs.q: During combustion, a substance reacts with:
mcqs.why: Combustion is the reaction of a substance (fuel) with oxygen, releasing heat and light energy.

mcqs.q: Silver + Hydrogen sulphide + Oxygen → Silver sulphide + Water. This reaction is known as:
mcqs.why: The black layer of silver sulphide dulls the surface of silver — this surface chemical change is called tarnishing; rusting is specific to iron.

mcqs.q: Rusting of iron requires contact with:
mcqs.why: Iron rusts only when both oxygen (air) and water/moisture are present; keeping iron dry or coated stops rusting.

mcqs.q: Galvanisation protects iron from rusting by coating it with:
mcqs.why: In galvanisation, iron is coated with a layer of zinc, which keeps air and moisture away and itself resists corrosion.

mcqs.q: The word equation for burning of methane (kitchen gas) is:
mcqs.why: Methane burns completely in oxygen (air) giving carbon dioxide and water vapour, along with heat and light.

mcqs.q: Nitrogen + Hydrogen → ?
mcqs.why: Under high pressure with a catalyst, nitrogen and hydrogen combine to form ammonia, used for making fertilisers.

mcqs.q: On heating, iron filings and sulphur combine to form:
mcqs.why: Heating iron with sulphur is a chemical change producing iron sulphide, a new substance with properties different from both elements.

lessons.title: Atoms, Molecules and Ions
lessons.notes_html:
Molecules

A molecule consists of two or more atoms joined together. A molecule of an element consists of atoms of the same kind only, e.g. O2, Cl2 and N2; one molecule of chlorine gas contains 2 atoms. A molecule of a compound consists of atoms of two or more different elements combined in a fixed ratio, e.g. H2O contains hydrogen and oxygen, and CO2 contains carbon and oxygen. Carbon tetrachloride, CCl4, contains two kinds of atoms: 1 atom of carbon and 4 atoms of chlorine — 5 atoms in total.

Symbols

A symbol represents one atom of an element: Copper = Cu, Iron = Fe, Chlorine = Cl, Potassium = K, Argon = Ar, Phosphorus = P, Beryllium = Be, Carbon = C, Calcium = Ca, Silicon = Si.

Ions: Cations and Anions

An ion is an atom or group of atoms carrying an electric charge, formed by loss or gain of electrons. A positive ion (cation) is formed when an atom loses electrons, e.g. Na+ and NH4+ (ammonium ion). A negative ion (anion) is formed when an atom gains electrons, e.g. Cl− (chloride ion) and S2−. Cations are mostly formed by metals and anions by non-metals. A symbol represents one atom of an element, while a formula represents a whole molecule or compound.

Key Points

  • A molecule has two or more atoms; element molecules have one kind of atom, compound molecules have different kinds.
  • Cations are positive (formed by losing electrons); anions are negative (formed by gaining electrons).
  • CCl4 contains 1 carbon atom and 4 chlorine atoms.

mcqs.q: A molecule consists of two or more:
mcqs.why: A molecule is a group of two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds, e.g. Cl2 has two chlorine atoms.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a cation?
mcqs.why: A cation carries a positive charge; the ammonium ion NH4+ is positively charged, while H2, H2O and CO2 are neutral molecules.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an anion?
mcqs.why: An anion carries a negative charge; the chloride ion Cl- is formed when a chlorine atom gains one electron.

mcqs.q: How many atoms form one molecule of chlorine gas?
mcqs.why: Chlorine gas is diatomic: each molecule, Cl2, consists of two chlorine atoms joined by a covalent bond.

mcqs.q: The number and kinds of atoms in carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) are:
options: 1 carbon and 4 chlorine — 5 atoms in total
mcqs.why: The subscript 4 applies to chlorine only: CCl4 has one carbon atom and four chlorine atoms, two kinds of atoms and five atoms altogether.

mcqs.q: A molecule of a compound differs from a molecule of an element because it contains:
options: atoms of two or more different elements in a fixed ratio
mcqs.why: H2O and CO2 are compound molecules with different kinds of atoms; O2 and N2 are element molecules with only one kind of atom.

mcqs.q: A positive ion (cation) is formed when an atom:
mcqs.why: Losing negatively charged electrons leaves the atom with more protons than electrons, so it becomes a positive ion, e.g. Na+.

mcqs.q: The symbol for potassium is:
mcqs.why: Potassium's symbol K comes from its Latin name Kalium; P is the symbol of phosphorus.

mcqs.q: The symbol for iron is:
mcqs.why: Iron's symbol Fe comes from its Latin name Ferrum; copper is Cu and calcium is Ca.

mcqs.q: A symbol differs from a formula because a symbol represents:
options: one atom of an element, while a formula represents a molecule or compound
mcqs.why: Na is the symbol of one sodium atom; NaCl is a formula showing all the atoms in one unit of the compound.

lessons.title: Valency and Electronic Configuration
lessons.notes_html:
Valency

Valency is the combining capacity of an atom of an element — the number of electrons an atom loses, gains or shares to complete its outer shell. Sodium has valency 1 (it loses 1 electron; its outermost shell has 1 electron), oxygen is a divalent element with valency 2, and aluminium has valency 3. The outermost shell of a chlorine atom has 7 electrons, so chlorine gains 1 electron to complete its shell.

Stable Electronic Configuration

Atoms form bonds to complete their outer shells and become stable. Helium (He) has a stable electronic configuration because its only shell is complete with 2 electrons, while H, C and Li have incomplete outer shells.

Electronic Configuration

Electronic configuration is the distribution of electrons of an atom in its shells around the nucleus, following the capacity 2n2 of each shell. Example: magnesium (12) is 2, 8, 2 and chlorine (17) is 2, 8, 7. It explains the valency and chemical behaviour of the element: magnesium loses its 2 outer electrons (valency 2) and chlorine gains 1 (valency 1).

Key Points

  • Valency = electrons lost, gained or shared to complete the outer shell.
  • Sodium: 1 electron in the outer shell, valency 1; chlorine: 7 outer electrons, valency 1; oxygen: valency 2.
  • Helium is stable because its shell is complete.

mcqs.q: Oxygen is a:
mcqs.why: Oxygen has 6 electrons in its outer shell and needs 2 more to complete it, so its combining capacity (valency) is 2 — it is divalent.

mcqs.q: The outermost shell of a sodium atom has ________ electron(s):
mcqs.why: Sodium (11) has configuration 2, 8, 1 — a single electron in its outermost shell, which it loses to form Na+.

mcqs.q: The outermost shell of a chlorine atom has ________ electrons:
mcqs.why: Chlorine (17) has configuration 2, 8, 7 — seven electrons in the outer shell, so it gains one electron to complete the octet.

mcqs.q: Which of the following has a stable electronic configuration?
mcqs.why: Helium's only shell is complete with 2 electrons, making it stable and unreactive; H (1), C (2,4) and Li (2,1) have incomplete outer shells.

mcqs.q: Valency is:
options: the number of protons in the nucleus
the number of shells in an atom
the combining capacity of an atom — the number of electrons it loses, gains or shares
mcqs.why: Valency measures how an atom combines: sodium has valency 1, oxygen 2 and aluminium 3, according to the electrons needed to complete the outer shell.

mcqs.q: The electronic configuration of magnesium (atomic number 12) is:
mcqs.why: The K shell holds 2, the L shell holds 8, and the remaining 2 electrons go into the M shell: 2, 8, 2 — giving magnesium valency 2.

mcqs.q: Aluminium has valency 3 because it:
options: loses its 3 outer electrons to complete its shell
mcqs.why: Aluminium (2, 8, 3) completes its outer shell by losing the 3 electrons of its M shell, forming Al3+ — hence valency 3.

mcqs.q: Electronic configuration explains an element's:
mcqs.why: Knowing how electrons are arranged in shells tells us how many an atom will lose, gain or share — its valency and reactivity.

mcqs.q: An atom becomes stable when:
mcqs.why: Atoms lose, gain or share electrons in chemical bonding precisely to complete their outer shells, like the noble gases.

mcqs.q: Chlorine forms the anion Cl- by:
options: gaining 1 electron to complete its outer shell
mcqs.why: With 7 outer electrons, chlorine needs just one more for a complete octet; gaining it gives the negative chloride ion Cl-.

lessons.title: Chemical Bonds and Formulae
lessons.notes_html:
Chemical Bonds

A bond (chemical bond) is the force of attraction that holds two or more atoms together in a molecule or compound. Atoms form bonds to complete their outer shells and become stable. In an ionic bond, electrons are transferred from one atom to another (e.g. sodium gives its outer electron to chlorine, forming Na+ and Cl− which attract each other). In a covalent bond, electrons are shared between atoms: a single bond shares one pair, a double bond shares two pairs (as in CO2) and a triple bond shares three pairs (as in N2). In a metallic bond, metal atoms release their outer electrons into a common 'sea' of free electrons around the positive metal ions; this explains why metals conduct electricity and heat, are malleable and ductile, and have high melting points.

Chemical Formulae

A chemical formula is the symbolic representation of a substance showing the kinds and numbers of atoms in it: H2O shows 2 atoms of hydrogen and 1 atom of oxygen; Ca(OH)2 shows one calcium, two oxygen and two hydrogen atoms. Important formulae: sodium bicarbonate = NaHCO3, calcium hydroxide = Ca(OH)2, ammonia = NH3, potassium chloride = KCl, acetic acid = CH3COOH, ammonium hydroxide = NH4OH, sulphuric acid = H2SO4, nitric acid = HNO3, benzene = C6H6, methane = CH4.

Key Points

  • Ionic bond = transfer of electrons; covalent bond = sharing of electrons.
  • N2 has a triple covalent bond; CO2 has double covalent bonds.
  • A formula shows the kinds and numbers of atoms in a substance.

mcqs.q: The chemical bond between the atoms in an N2 molecule is:
mcqs.why: Each nitrogen atom shares three pairs of electrons with the other, forming a triple covalent bond in N2.

mcqs.q: Which of the following has a double covalent bond?
mcqs.why: In carbon dioxide, carbon shares two pairs of electrons with each oxygen atom (double bonds); N2 has a triple bond and Br2 and HCl have single bonds.

mcqs.q: A chemical bond is:
options: the force of attraction that holds atoms together in a molecule or compound
mcqs.why: Atoms form bonds — by transferring or sharing electrons — to complete their outer shells and become stable.

mcqs.q: In an ionic bond, atoms are held together after:
options: transfer of electrons from one atom to another, forming oppositely charged ions
mcqs.why: In NaCl, sodium transfers its outer electron to chlorine; the resulting Na+ and Cl- ions attract each other — the ionic bond.

mcqs.q: The chemical formula of sulphuric acid is:
mcqs.why: Sulphuric acid is H2SO4 — 2 hydrogen, 1 sulphur and 4 oxygen atoms; HNO3 is nitric acid and CH3COOH is acetic acid.

mcqs.q: The formula Ca(OH)2 shows that one unit of calcium hydroxide contains:
options: one calcium, two oxygen and two hydrogen atoms
two calcium, one oxygen and two hydrogen atoms
one calcium, one oxygen and two hydrogen atoms
two calcium and two hydrogen atoms only
mcqs.why: The subscript 2 outside the bracket doubles everything inside (OH): one Ca, two O and two H atoms.

mcqs.q: The chemical formula of ammonia is:
mcqs.why: Ammonia is NH3 — one nitrogen atom joined to three hydrogen atoms; NH4OH is ammonium hydroxide and CH4 is methane.

mcqs.q: Metals conduct electricity well because of the metallic bond, in which:
options: outer electrons form a free-moving 'sea' around the positive metal ions
mcqs.why: The attraction between positive metal ions and the sea of free electrons is the metallic bond; the free electrons carry electric current and heat.

mcqs.q: The formula of sodium bicarbonate is:
mcqs.why: Sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) is NaHCO3; KCl is potassium chloride and NaOH is sodium hydroxide.

mcqs.q: Atoms form chemical bonds mainly to:
options: complete their outer shells and become stable
mcqs.why: By losing, gaining or sharing electrons in bonding, atoms achieve a complete outer shell like the stable noble gases.

lessons.title: Solute, Solvent and Types of Solutions
lessons.notes_html:
Parts of a Solution

A solution is a homogeneous mixture — it has the same composition and properties throughout, and its components cannot be seen separately. The solute is the component dissolved in the solvent, usually present in the smaller amount (in salt solution, common salt is the solute). The solvent is the component that dissolves the solute. A solution made of only two components — one solute and one solvent — is a binary solution. A solution in which water is the solvent is an aqueous solution; water is called the universal solvent because it dissolves a large number of substances. Oil is insoluble in water.

Dilute, Concentrated, Unsaturated and Saturated

A dilute solution has a relatively small amount of solute dissolved in it, while a concentrated solution has a large amount — though it can still dissolve a little more solute. An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at a particular temperature. A saturated solution is one to which no more solute can be dissolved at that temperature.

Preparing a Solution

Take a measured amount of solvent in a clean beaker and add the solute in small portions, stirring well with a glass rod after each addition so the solute dissolves completely. Continue until the required amount has dissolved; the uniform mixture obtained is the solution.

Key Points

  • Solute = the dissolved component (smaller amount); solvent = the dissolving component.
  • A binary solution has exactly two components; an aqueous solution has water as solvent.
  • A saturated solution can dissolve no more solute at that temperature.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is insoluble in water?
mcqs.why: Oil does not dissolve in water and forms a separate layer; sodium chloride (table salt) and baking powder dissolve in water.

mcqs.q: A solution to which no more solute can be dissolved at a particular temperature is called a:
mcqs.why: A saturated solution already holds the maximum amount of solute at that temperature; any extra solute stays undissolved.

mcqs.q: A concentrated solution can dissolve in it:
options: amount of solute equal to the amount of solvent
mcqs.why: A concentrated solution already has much solute, so only a smaller (less) further quantity can dissolve before saturation; a saturated solution can dissolve none.

mcqs.q: A solution having a relatively less amount of solute dissolved in it is called a:
mcqs.why: Dilute means little solute in much solvent; a concentrated solution has a relatively large amount of solute.

mcqs.q: In salt solution, the solute is:
mcqs.why: The solute is the component that dissolves and is present in the smaller amount — the salt; water is the solvent.

mcqs.q: A binary solution is a solution made of:
options: only two components — one solute and one solvent
mcqs.why: Binary means two: a binary solution contains exactly one solute dissolved in one solvent, e.g. salt in water.

mcqs.q: An aqueous solution is one in which the solvent is:
