mcqs.why: Aqueous solutions use water as the solvent — e.g. sugar solution and lemon water; water is called the universal solvent.

mcqs.q: A homogeneous mixture is one in which:
options: the components can be seen separately
the composition and properties are the same throughout
mcqs.why: A true solution is homogeneous: it looks uniform from top to bottom and its components cannot be seen separately.

mcqs.q: An unsaturated solution is one which:
options: can dissolve more solute at a particular temperature
mcqs.why: More solute added to an unsaturated solution dissolves completely until the solution becomes saturated.

mcqs.q: To prepare a solution properly, the solute should be:
options: added in small portions with stirring so it dissolves completely
added all at once without stirring
mcqs.why: Adding the solute gradually and stirring with a glass rod makes it dissolve fully and gives a uniform solution.

lessons.title: Solubility and Its Importance
lessons.notes_html:
Solubility

The amount of solute required to saturate 100 g of solvent at a particular temperature is called its solubility. Solubility depends on the nature of the solute and solvent ('like dissolves like' — oil does not dissolve in water). Temperature: the solubility of most solids increases with rise in temperature, while that of gases decreases. Pressure affects the solubility of gases — more pressure dissolves more gas, as in soft drinks. Particle size and stirring do not change solubility itself but make dissolving faster. The solubility of table salt increases only very slightly with temperature: about 36 g of salt saturates 100 g of water at room temperature, unlike sugar or potassium nitrate, whose solubility increases greatly on heating.

Making Dissolving Faster

Dissolution becomes faster by (i) stirring the mixture, (ii) heating the solvent, and (iii) using the solute in powdered (small particle) form, which increases its surface area. These methods increase the speed of dissolving, though the total amount that can dissolve at saturation is fixed at a given temperature.

Importance of Solutions

Solutions are used everywhere: medicines are given as solutions and syrups; soft drinks and juices are solutions; seawater is a natural solution; soaps and detergents work as solutions; fertilisers are applied in solution; blood carries food and oxygen in solution; and the textile, paint and pharmaceutical industries depend on them. In textiles, dyes must dissolve properly to colour cloth evenly; in pharmaceuticals, medicines must dissolve in body fluids to be absorbed and to act. Rock candy shows crystallisation from solution: as a hot saturated sugar solution cools and water evaporates, its solubility decreases and sugar crystals grow on the sticks.

Key Points

  • Solubility = grams of solute needed to saturate 100 g of solvent at a given temperature.
  • Heating increases the solubility of most solids but decreases that of gases; pressure increases gas solubility.
  • Stirring, heating and powdering speed up dissolving but do not change solubility.

mcqs.q: The amount of solute required to saturate 100 g of solvent at a particular temperature is called:
mcqs.why: Solubility is defined per 100 g of solvent at a stated temperature — the amount that just makes a saturated solution.

mcqs.q: The solubility of table salt in water, on heating, increases:
options: not at all in any liquid
mcqs.why: About 36 g of salt saturates 100 g of water at room temperature and heating dissolves only a little more — unlike sugar or potassium nitrate.

mcqs.q: The solubility of gases in water decreases when:
mcqs.why: Gases escape from warm liquids, so their solubility falls as temperature rises — the opposite behaviour to most solids.

mcqs.q: More gas dissolves in a soft drink because of:
options: high pressure in the sealed bottle
mcqs.why: Pressure increases the solubility of gases; carbon dioxide is forced into soft drinks under high pressure and escapes as fizz when the bottle opens.

mcqs.q: Dissolving becomes faster when we:
options: use one big lump of solute
keep the mixture still and cold
stir the mixture, heat the solvent and use powdered solute
mcqs.why: Stirring, heating and a larger surface area (powder) all speed up dissolving, though the solubility limit itself stays fixed at that temperature.

mcqs.q: Stirring a solution changes:
options: the speed of dissolving, not the solubility
mcqs.why: Stirring only brings fresh solvent into contact with the solute faster; the maximum amount that can dissolve at that temperature is unchanged.

mcqs.q: Rock candy crystals grow on sticks in a cooling saturated sugar solution because:
options: the solubility of sugar decreases on cooling, so extra sugar crystallises out
mcqs.why: A hot saturated solution holds more sugar than a cold one; as it cools and evaporates, the excess sugar deposits as crystals on the sticks.

mcqs.q: In the pharmaceutical industry, solubility matters because medicines must:
options: dissolve in body fluids to be absorbed and to act
mcqs.why: A medicine can be absorbed and work only if it dissolves properly; solubility is controlled in syrups, injections and tablets.

mcqs.q: In the textile industry, dyes must dissolve properly in water so that:
options: the dye lasts forever without washing
mcqs.why: Even colouring needs the dye uniformly dissolved; solubility decides which dye suits which fabric and how fast the colour will be.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a natural solution?
mcqs.why: Seawater is a natural homogeneous solution of many salts in water; blood, soft drinks and fertiliser solutions are other everyday solutions.

lessons.title: Contact and Non-contact Forces
lessons.notes_html:
Contact Forces

Forces that act only when two objects are physically in contact with each other are called contact forces. Examples: muscular force, frictional force, and the push or pull applied by hand.

Non-contact Forces

Forces that act on objects without physical contact, from a distance, are called non-contact forces. Examples: gravitational force, magnetic force and electrostatic force. Gravitational force is the force of attraction between any two masses; the Earth's pull on objects is called gravity, and this pull on an object is also its weight. Its value increases with mass and decreases with distance.

Non-contact Forces at Work

Gravity pulls a ripe apple down from the tree without contact, and keeps pulling a kicked football down along a curved path. A magnet attracts iron pins from a distance, and like poles of two magnets repel each other without touching. A charged comb attracts small pieces of paper by electrostatic force. A porter carrying a load feels gravity pulling the load downwards as its weight. A rocket leaving the launching pad experiences the upward thrust of its burning fuel gases and the downward gravitational force (weight); it rises because the thrust is greater than its weight, with air resistance also acting downwards.

Key Points

  • Contact forces need touch (muscular force, friction); non-contact forces act at a distance (gravity, magnetism, electrostatic force).
  • Gravity is the Earth's pull on objects; the force between two negatively charged particles is repulsion.
  • A rocket rises when its upward thrust exceeds its weight.

mcqs.q: An example of a contact force is:
mcqs.why: Muscular force acts only when the muscles touch the object; gravity, magnetism and electrostatic force act from a distance without contact.

mcqs.q: The force between two negatively charged particles is:
mcqs.why: Like charges repel each other: two negatively charged particles push each other away by electrostatic repulsion.

mcqs.q: The Earth's pull on objects is called:
mcqs.why: Gravity is the Earth's gravitational pull attracting all objects towards its centre; this pull on an object is also called its weight.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a non-contact force?
mcqs.why: A magnet attracts iron pins from a distance without touching them, so magnetic force is a non-contact force.

mcqs.q: Contact forces act only when:
options: two objects are physically in contact with each other
mcqs.why: Muscular force and friction require actual touch between the objects; without contact they cannot act.

mcqs.q: Gravitational force is the force of attraction between:
mcqs.why: Every pair of masses attracts each other gravitationally; the force increases with mass and decreases with distance.

mcqs.q: A charged comb attracts small pieces of paper by:
mcqs.why: The charged comb exerts an electrostatic force that pulls the light, neutral paper pieces towards it from a small distance.

mcqs.q: Immediately after leaving the launching pad, the two main forces on a rising rocket are:
options: upward thrust of the escaping gases and downward gravitational force (weight)
mcqs.why: The burning fuel pushes gases down and the rocket up (thrust), while gravity pulls it down; it rises because thrust exceeds weight.

mcqs.q: When like poles of two magnets are brought near each other, they:
mcqs.why: Like magnetic poles repel — a non-contact magnetic force pushes the magnets apart before they touch.

mcqs.q: A ripe apple falls from a tree because of:
options: the Earth's gravity pulling it down without contact
mcqs.why: Gravity acts at a distance and pulls the apple towards the Earth as soon as it separates from the branch.

lessons.title: Effects of Force and Action–Reaction
lessons.notes_html:
Effects of a Force

A force can change the shape of an object, change its direction of motion, bring a moving object to rest, or set a resting object into motion. When a batsman hits the ball back towards the bowler, the effect seen is a change of direction of the moving ball.

Newton's Third Law: Action and Reaction

For every action force, there is an equivalent (equal) reaction force in the opposite direction. The reaction is not smaller than the action, and it acts in the opposite — not the same — direction. This is how a rocket rises: the gases are pushed downwards (action) and the rocket is pushed upwards (reaction).

Units and Statements

The SI unit of force is the newton (N). Remember: 1 m is not 1000 km (1 km = 1000 m), m/s is the unit of speed (not displacement), and 1 hour = 3600 seconds (not 60 s).

Key Points

  • Force can change shape, direction, speed or state of rest/motion of an object.
  • Action and reaction are equal in size and opposite in direction.
  • The unit of force is the newton (N).

mcqs.q: Which statement is true?
options: for every action force, there is a smaller reaction force in the opposite direction
for every action force, there is a smaller reaction force in the same direction
for every action force, there is an equivalent reaction force in opposite direction
for every action force, there is an equivalent reaction force in the same direction
mcqs.why: Newton's third law: action and reaction are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction; the reaction is never smaller than the action.

mcqs.q: A batsman hits the ball back towards the bowler; which effect of force is seen?
options: change of state from motion to rest
change of state from rest to motion
mcqs.why: The moving ball reverses its path when struck, so the applied force has changed the direction of its motion.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: m/s is the unit of displacement
N is the unit of force
mcqs.why: The newton (N) is the SI unit of force. In fact 1 km = 1000 m, m/s is the unit of speed, and 1 hour = 3600 seconds.

mcqs.q: Pressing a lump of clay flat shows which effect of force?
mcqs.why: The applied force deforms the clay without moving it as a whole — a change of shape is one of the effects of force.

mcqs.q: A force applied to a stationary football by a kick shows the effect of:
options: change of state from rest to motion
mcqs.why: The kick sets the resting ball moving — force can change an object's state from rest to motion.

mcqs.q: A goalkeeper catching a fast ball shows the effect of force as:
options: change of shape of the ball
change of state from motion to rest
mcqs.why: The force applied by the hands overcomes the ball's motion and brings it to rest.

mcqs.q: The reaction force is always:
options: equal to the action force and in the opposite direction
in the same direction as the action
mcqs.why: Action and reaction form an equal and opposite pair acting on different bodies — neither is smaller than the other.

mcqs.q: A rocket rises because:
options: the downward push of escaping gases produces an upward reaction force greater than its weight
mcqs.why: By action–reaction, gases forced downwards push the rocket upwards; when this thrust exceeds the weight, the rocket lifts off.

mcqs.q: Which is the SI unit of force?
mcqs.why: Force is measured in newtons (N), named after Isaac Newton; the metre measures length and the kilogram measures mass.

mcqs.q: 1 hour is equal to:
mcqs.why: 1 hour = 60 minutes and each minute has 60 seconds, so 1 hour = 60 × 60 = 3600 seconds.

lessons.title: Speed and Displacement
lessons.notes_html:
Displacement

Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance between the starting point and the final position of a moving object, measured in a specified direction. Its SI unit is the metre (m). Displacement is not 'the distance covered in one second' — that idea belongs to speed.

Speed

Speed is the distance covered by a moving object in unit time: speed = distance / time. Its SI unit is metre per second (m/s); kilometre per hour (km/h) is commonly used for vehicles.

Worked Examples

Car journey: A car makes a 12-hour journey at an average speed of 60 km/h. Total distance = 60 × 12 = 720 km. The last two parts cover 240 + 240 = 480 km, so the first part X = 720 − 480 = 240 km.

Toy train: A toy train runs down a slope covering 10 m every 2 seconds (0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 m at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 s). Its distance–time graph is a straight line through the origin, showing uniform motion at a constant speed of 50 ÷ 10 = 5 m/s; it covers 5 m in the first second and 10 m between 2 s and 4 s, and again 10 m between 8 s and 10 s.

Walking speed: Walking fast along a 30 m track in an average time of 12 s gives speed = 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5 m/s.

Key Points

  • Displacement = shortest distance in a specified direction, unit metre.
  • Speed = distance ÷ time, unit m/s.
  • A straight-line distance–time graph through the origin shows uniform (constant) speed.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following statements is NOT correct?
options: Displacement is the distance covered in one second
Displacement is the shortest distance between two points
Metre (m) is the unit of displacement
Rate of change of distance with time is called speed
mcqs.why: Distance covered in one second describes speed, not displacement. Displacement is the shortest straight-line distance between start and finish, in metres.

mcqs.q: Speed is calculated by:
mcqs.why: Speed = distance covered ÷ time taken; its SI unit is metre per second (m/s).

mcqs.q: A car travels for 12 hours at an average speed of 60 km/h. Two parts of the journey cover 240 km and 240 km. The remaining part X is:
A toy train covers 50 m in 10 s at a constant rate. Its speed is:
mcqs.why: Speed = distance ÷ time = 50 ÷ 10 = 5 m/s. The train covers equal distances (5 m) in every second — uniform motion.

mcqs.q: The distance–time graph of the toy train is a straight line through the origin. This shows:
options: the train moves with uniform (constant) speed
mcqs.why: Equal distances in equal time intervals give a straight-line graph; its constant slope is the constant speed of 5 m/s.

mcqs.q: A student walks a 30 m track in an average time of 12 s. Her average speed is:
mcqs.why: Average speed = distance ÷ time = 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5 m/s.

mcqs.q: Displacement must always be stated with its:
mcqs.why: Displacement is measured in a specified direction from the starting point to the final position; distance alone does not need a direction.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of speed is:
mcqs.why: Speed is distance (metres) divided by time (seconds), giving m/s as the SI unit; km/h is a common practical unit for vehicles.

mcqs.q: A cyclist covers 100 m in 20 s. His speed is:
mcqs.why: Speed = distance ÷ time = 100 ÷ 20 = 5 m/s, using the SI units of metres and seconds.

mcqs.q: If an object returns to its starting point after a journey, its displacement is:
options: equal to the total distance covered
mcqs.why: Displacement is the shortest distance between the starting and final positions; if both are the same point, the displacement is zero even though distance was covered.

lessons.title: Waves and Their Features
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Wave?

A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter. Waves are produced by vibrations. They may be mechanical waves, which need a medium (e.g. sound), or electromagnetic waves, which need no medium (e.g. light).

Features of a Wave

Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive crests (or two consecutive troughs) of a transverse wave, or between two consecutive compressions of a longitudinal wave; it is measured in metres. Amplitude is the maximum displacement (height) of the wave from its rest position or midline; for sound, greater amplitude means a louder sound. Frequency is the number of complete waves passing a point in one second; its unit is the hertz (Hz). Time period is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point; T = 1/f. On a printed transverse-wave figure, the highest point is the crest, the lowest is the trough, amplitude is read from the midline to a crest, and wavelength from one crest to the next.

Key Points

  • Waves transfer energy, not matter.
  • Wavelength = crest-to-crest distance; amplitude = height from the midline.
  • Frequency = waves per second (Hz); time period T = 1/f.

mcqs.q: Which feature is the height of the wave from the rest position or midline?
mcqs.why: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a wave from its rest position; for sound, a greater amplitude gives a louder sound.

mcqs.q: Which feature of a wave is the number of waves that pass by each second?
mcqs.why: Frequency counts the complete waves passing a point in one second and is measured in hertz (Hz).

mcqs.q: What is transferred by the movement of waves?
mcqs.why: A wave is a disturbance that carries energy from place to place while the particles of the medium only vibrate about their positions.

mcqs.q: Wavelength is the distance between:
options: a crest and the nearest trough
two consecutive crests or two consecutive troughs
two compressions of a transverse wave only
mcqs.why: One complete wave spans from one crest to the next crest (or trough to trough); in a longitudinal wave it is measured between consecutive compressions.

mcqs.q: The time period of a wave is:
options: the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point
the number of waves per second
mcqs.why: Time period T is the duration of one complete vibration, measured in seconds, and T = 1/f where f is the frequency.

mcqs.q: If a wave has a frequency of 5 Hz, its time period is:
mcqs.why: T = 1/f = 1 ÷ 5 = 0.2 s. Each of the five waves passing per second takes one-fifth of a second.

mcqs.q: The highest point of a transverse wave is called the:
mcqs.why: The crest is the topmost point of a transverse wave and the trough is the lowest point; compressions and rarefactions belong to longitudinal waves.

mcqs.q: The unit of frequency is the:
mcqs.why: Frequency — waves per second — is measured in hertz; one hertz means one complete wave passing per second.

mcqs.q: For a sound wave, a greater amplitude means:
mcqs.why: Loudness depends on amplitude: bigger vibrations produce louder sounds, while pitch depends on frequency.

mcqs.q: Waves are produced by:
mcqs.why: Every wave begins with a vibration — of a string, of air particles, or of an electric field — which passes energy onward.

lessons.title: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves
lessons.notes_html:
Transverse Waves

In a transverse wave the particles of the medium vibrate at right angles to the direction of the wave, forming crests and troughs — e.g. water waves and light. Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves that do not need any material medium and can travel through vacuum at the speed of light; examples are light, radio waves, X-rays and ultraviolet rays.

Longitudinal Waves

In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate back and forth along the direction of the wave, forming compressions and rarefactions. Sound waves are longitudinal and mechanical: they need a medium and cannot pass through a vacuum. Sound is longitudinal because the vibrating source pushes the air particles back and forth in the same direction as the sound travels.

The Visible Spectrum

The sequence of visible colours from longest wavelength to shortest wavelength is: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. Red light has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest.

Key Points

  • Transverse: particles vibrate at right angles to travel — crests and troughs (light, water waves).
  • Longitudinal: particles vibrate along the direction of travel — compressions and rarefactions (sound).
  • Electromagnetic waves need no medium; mechanical waves (sound) do.

mcqs.q: Sound waves are not:
mcqs.why: Sound is a longitudinal (compressional) mechanical wave: air particles vibrate along the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions.

mcqs.q: Sound cannot pass through:
mcqs.why: Sound is a mechanical wave needing a material medium; in a vacuum there are no particles to vibrate, so sound cannot travel.

mcqs.q: What type of wave does not need matter to travel through?
mcqs.why: Electromagnetic waves such as light can travel through empty space (vacuum) at the speed of light; mechanical waves need a medium.

mcqs.q: Which sequence of visible colour is correct from longest wavelength to short wavelength?
options: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet
violet, indigo, blue, green, orange, yellow, red
red, yellow, green, orange, violet, blue, indigo
red, yellow, green, orange, violet, indigo, blue
mcqs.why: In the visible spectrum, red has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest, with orange, yellow, green, blue and indigo in between.

mcqs.q: In a transverse wave, the particles of the medium vibrate:
options: along the direction of the wave
at right angles to the direction of the wave
mcqs.why: Transverse waves form crests and troughs because the particles move up and down, perpendicular to the wave's travel.

mcqs.q: Sound is considered a longitudinal wave because:
options: air particles vibrate back and forth in the same direction as the sound travels
mcqs.why: The vibrating source pushes air particles parallel to the direction of propagation, producing compressions and rarefactions — the mark of a longitudinal wave.

mcqs.q: Compressions and rarefactions are features of:
mcqs.why: Where particles are pushed together (compression) and spread apart (rarefaction), the wave is longitudinal — as in sound travelling through air.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an electromagnetic wave?
mcqs.why: X-rays, like light, radio waves and ultraviolet rays, are electromagnetic waves that need no medium; sound and water waves are mechanical.

mcqs.q: Light travels through vacuum at:
options: the speed of light — the fastest possible speed
mcqs.why: Electromagnetic waves travel through vacuum at the speed of light, far faster than sound's 340 m/s in air.

mcqs.q: A water wave on a pond is an example of a:
mcqs.why: In water waves the surface moves up and down (crests and troughs) at right angles to the direction the wave travels.

lessons.title: Sound and Hearing
lessons.notes_html:
Sound in Air

The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s. Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases but not through a vacuum.

Loudness and Pitch

Sounds differ in loudness and pitch. A whisper is a soft sound of low loudness, while a loudspeaker at full volume or thunder is loud — loudness depends on amplitude. The sound of a drum or a man's voice is low-pitched, while a whistle or a bird's chirp is high-pitched — pitch depends on frequency. High-pitched, loud sounds such as sirens of ambulances, police vehicles and fire brigades, alarm bells and whistles are used in emergencies because their sharp pitch and loudness attract immediate attention.

Audible Sound

Audible sound is the sound that can be heard by the human ear. The audible frequency range of a normal human ear is from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). Sounds below 20 Hz are called infrasound and those above 20,000 Hz are called ultrasound; neither can be heard by humans. A weak sound is heard easily at night because there is little background noise to mask it and sound travels well in the cool night air, while daytime traffic, machines and voices hide it.

Key Points

  • Speed of sound in air = 340 m/s; sound needs a medium.
  • Loudness depends on amplitude; pitch depends on frequency.
  • Human hearing range: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; below is infrasound, above is ultrasound.

mcqs.q: The speed of sound in air is:
mcqs.why: Sound travels through air at about 340 metres per second — much slower than light, which is why thunder is heard after lightning is seen.

mcqs.q: The audible frequency range of a normal human ear is:
mcqs.why: Humans hear sounds between 20 Hz and 20,000 Hz (20 kHz); below 20 Hz is infrasound and above 20 kHz is ultrasound.

mcqs.q: Sounds with a frequency above 20,000 Hz are called:
mcqs.why: Ultrasound lies above the human hearing limit and is used in medical scans and SONAR; infrasound lies below 20 Hz.

mcqs.q: The pitch of a sound depends on its:
mcqs.why: High-frequency vibrations give high-pitched sounds like a whistle; low frequencies give low-pitched sounds like a drum. Loudness depends on amplitude.

mcqs.q: Which pair correctly matches the sound with its quality?
mcqs.why: A whisper has small amplitude and low loudness, thunder is loud, and a bird's chirp is high-pitched, not low-pitched.

mcqs.q: Sirens of ambulances and fire brigades are used in emergencies because they are:
options: high-pitched and loud, attracting immediate attention from a distance
mcqs.why: Sharp pitch and great loudness make sirens, alarm bells and whistles heard far away, warning people to give way or act quickly.

mcqs.q: A very weak sound is heard easily at night but not during the day because:
options: our ears grow bigger at night
there is little background noise at night to mask it
mcqs.why: Daytime traffic, machines and voices mask weak sounds; in the quiet of night, with sound travelling well in cool air, weak sounds reach the ears clearly.

mcqs.q: Sound travels fastest through:
options: it travels equally in all media
mcqs.why: Particles are closest together in solids, so vibrations pass on quickest; sound is slower in liquids, slower still in gases, and impossible in a vacuum.

mcqs.q: An echo is produced when sound:
options: is absorbed by a soft surface
reflects from a hard surface such as a wall or cliff
mcqs.why: Sound waves bounce off hard surfaces; the reflected sound heard separately is the echo, used in SONAR and by bats.

mcqs.q: Which of these sounds is infrasound for humans?
mcqs.why: Infrasound is below the 20 Hz lower limit of human hearing; 10 Hz vibrations (e.g. from elephants' calls) cannot be heard by us.

lessons.title: Hearing in Animals and Uses of Sound
lessons.notes_html:
Hearing Ranges of Animals

Animals hear ranges different from ours. The elephant can respond to the lowest frequencies (infrasound), while the dolphin can respond to the highest frequencies. A bat hears and produces sounds from about 2 kHz to 120 kHz — mostly ultrasound for humans — and uses the echoes to locate prey and obstacles while flying at night (echolocation). We cannot hear the bat's whistle because its frequency is above 20,000 Hz, beyond the audible range of the human ear.

Animals Without Ears

Snakes, fish, frogs and locusts have no outer ears but detect sound through vibrations: a snake senses ground vibrations through its jaw bones connected to the inner ear; fish detect vibrations in water through their lateral line system and inner ear; a frog has a flat eardrum (tympanum) on the surface of its head; a locust has hearing organs (tympana) on its abdomen and legs.

Communication and Uses of Sound

Animals communicate through sound: a hen calls her chicks with one sound and warns them of danger with another; dogs bark differently at strangers and at their owners; birds sing to mark territory and attract mates; elephants and whales send low-frequency calls over long distances. Sound is used for communication, alarms and sirens, music, medical imaging (ultrasound scans), SONAR to find objects under water and measure sea depth, cleaning delicate instruments by ultrasound, and echolocation by bats and dolphins.

Key Points

  • Elephants respond to the lowest frequencies; dolphins to the highest; bats hear 2 kHz–120 kHz.
  • The bat's whistle is ultrasound — inaudible to humans.
  • Sound is used in communication, alarms, ultrasound scans, SONAR and echolocation.

mcqs.q: Which of the following animals can respond to the lowest frequency?
mcqs.why: Elephants communicate with infrasound — very low-frequency calls that travel long distances and lie below the human hearing range.

mcqs.q: Which of the following animals can respond to the highest frequency?
mcqs.why: Dolphins respond to the highest frequencies of the animals listed, using high-pitched clicks and their echoes to navigate and hunt.

mcqs.q: Which animal has an audible range from 2 kHz to 120 kHz?
mcqs.why: A bat hears and produces sounds from about 2 kHz up to 120 kHz, using these ultrasound echoes for echolocation at night.

mcqs.q: We cannot hear the whistle of a bat because:
options: its frequency is higher than 20,000 Hz, above our audible range
mcqs.why: The bat's whistle is ultrasound; human ears respond only up to 20 kHz, so the sound is silent for us though other bats hear it clearly.

mcqs.q: Bats locate prey and obstacles at night by:
options: echolocation — listening to echoes of their ultrasound calls
mcqs.why: A bat emits ultrasound pulses and judges the position of objects from the returning echoes — the same principle as SONAR.

mcqs.q: SONAR is used to:
options: find objects under water and measure the depth of the sea
mcqs.why: SONAR sends sound pulses into water and times their echoes to locate submarines, shoals of fish and the sea bed.

mcqs.q: A snake, which has no outer ear, detects sound mainly through:
options: ground vibrations sensed through its jaw bones
mcqs.why: The snake's jaw bones, connected to the inner ear, pick up vibrations from the ground — its way of 'hearing'.

mcqs.q: Ultrasound scans are used in hospitals to:
options: make images of internal organs and unborn babies safely
mcqs.why: Reflected ultrasound waves build pictures of soft internal structures without harmful radiation — an important medical use of sound.

mcqs.q: Which observation proves that animals communicate with one another through sound?
options: a hen's danger call makes her chicks hide, while her food call gathers them
mcqs.why: Different calls producing fixed, different responses in other animals show the sounds carry definite meanings — true communication.

mcqs.q: Fish detect vibrations in water through:
options: their lateral line system and inner ear
mcqs.why: Fish have no outer ears; the lateral line senses vibrations and pressure changes in the water, working with the inner ear.

lessons.title: Heat and Temperature
lessons.notes_html:
Temperature

Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body. It is the average kinetic energy of the molecules of a substance: the faster the particles move and vibrate, the greater their average kinetic energy and the higher the temperature.

Heat

Heat is the form of energy that flows from a hot object to a cold object because of the difference of temperature between them. It is the total kinetic energy of the molecules of a substance and is measured in joules. The energy that transfers from one object to another due to a temperature difference is called heat energy.

Temperature Scales and the Thermometer

The Celsius (centigrade) and Fahrenheit scales are based on two fixed temperatures: the melting point of ice and the boiling point of water. On the Celsius scale these are 0°C and 100°C; on the Fahrenheit scale they are 32°F and 212°F. So the temperature of melting ice in the Fahrenheit scale is 32°F, and boiling water is 100°C in the centigrade scale. A thermometer's bulb is filled with a liquid such as alcohol (or mercury), which rises in the thin tube when it expands on heating.

Key Points

  • Temperature = degree of hotness or coldness = average kinetic energy of molecules.
  • Heat flows from hot to cold bodies because of a temperature difference.
  • Ice melts at 0°C = 32°F; water boils at 100°C = 212°F.

mcqs.q: The degree of hotness or coldness is called:
mcqs.why: Temperature measures how hot or cold a body is; heat is the energy that flows because of a temperature difference.

mcqs.q: The bulb of the thermometer is filled with:
mcqs.why: Liquid thermometers use alcohol (or mercury) in the bulb; the liquid expands and rises in the capillary tube as temperature rises.

mcqs.q: The centigrade scale is also called the:
mcqs.why: Centigrade and Celsius are two names for the same scale, on which ice melts at 0 and water boils at 100.

mcqs.q: The temperature of boiling water in the centigrade scale is:
mcqs.why: At standard atmospheric pressure, water boils at 100 on the Celsius (centigrade) scale — one of its two fixed points.

mcqs.q: The temperature of melting ice in the Fahrenheit scale is:
mcqs.why: On the Fahrenheit scale the melting point of ice is 32°F and the boiling point of water is 212°F.

mcqs.q: The average energy due to the movement of molecules in a substance is called:
mcqs.why: Temperature is the average kinetic energy of the particles; the faster they move, the hotter the substance.

mcqs.q: The energy that transfers from one object to another due to the temperature difference is called:
mcqs.why: Heat energy flows from the hotter object to the colder one until their temperatures become equal.

mcqs.q: Heat is measured in:
mcqs.why: Heat is a form of energy and all energy is measured in joules; degrees Celsius measure temperature, not heat.

mcqs.q: The two fixed temperatures on which the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales are based are:
options: the freezing of alcohol and boiling of oil
the melting point of ice and the boiling point of water
mcqs.why: Both scales are fixed by the melting point of ice (0°C / 32°F) and the boiling point of water (100°C / 212°F) at standard pressure.

mcqs.q: When the molecules of a substance move faster, the substance's:
mcqs.why: Greater average kinetic energy of the particles means a higher temperature; heating a substance makes its particles move faster.

lessons.title: Expansion and Contraction
lessons.notes_html:
Expansion on Heating, Contraction on Cooling

When a substance is heated, its particles gain kinetic energy and move farther apart, so the substance expands — a heated 10 cm iron rod increases in volume. On cooling, the particles lose energy and the inter-particle distances decrease, so the substance contracts. Different substances expand at different rates because the forces between their particles and their arrangements differ; e.g. alcohol expands more than glass, and brass more than iron. Gases expand the fastest on heating, liquids expand less and solids the least, because gas particles are far apart and held by very weak forces.

Uses of Expansion and Contraction

The thermometer works on expansion: the liquid expands and rises in the capillary tube on heating and contracts and falls on cooling, and the height of the column shows the temperature. Gaps are left after every few metres in railway tracks so the rails can expand in summer without bending and de-tracking. Expansion is also used in fixing metal tyres on cart wheels (a heated ring expands, fits, then contracts and grips) and in riveting; a bimetallic strip bends on heating and is used in thermostats and fire alarms. Expansion of liquids is used in liquid thermometers and some temperature switches. If an empty steel container is sealed and heated, the gas inside cannot expand, so its pressure increases.

Hot Air Balloons and the Peculiar Behaviour of Water

The air inside a hot air balloon is heated and expands, becoming less dense than the cold air outside, so the upthrust of the denser air lifts the balloon; when the air cools and contracts, the balloon descends. Water behaves peculiarly: it contracts on cooling only down to 4°C; below 4°C it expands, and on freezing it expands further, so ice is less dense than water and floats. This is why water pipes burst in severe winter and why lakes freeze from the top, leaving liquid water below in which fish survive.

Key Points

  • Heating increases inter-particle distances (expansion); cooling decreases them (contraction).
  • Gases expand most, liquids less, solids least.
  • Railway gaps, thermometers and hot air balloons all use expansion; water expands below 4°C.

mcqs.q: When a 10 cm iron rod is heated to a high temperature:
mcqs.why: On heating, the particles of the iron move farther apart, so the rod expands and its volume increases while its mass stays the same.

mcqs.q: The gaps are left after every few metres in the railway tracks so that:
options: they cannot be de-tracked in winter due to expansion
they cannot be de-tracked in summer due to expansion
they cannot be de-tracked in summer due to contraction
they cannot be de-tracked at night due to contraction
mcqs.why: In hot weather the rails expand; the gaps give them room to expand without buckling and pushing the train off the track.

mcqs.q: The rise of liquid in the thermometer is due to:
mcqs.why: The liquid in the thermometer expands on heating and rises in the thin capillary tube; on cooling it contracts and falls.

mcqs.q: The contraction of objects on cooling is due to:
options: reduction in size of the particles
increase in size of the particles
mcqs.why: The particles themselves do not shrink; on cooling they lose energy and come closer together, so the whole object contracts.

mcqs.q: An empty steel container is sealed and heated; which property of the gas is likely to increase?
mcqs.why: The sealed container keeps the volume fixed, so the faster-moving gas particles collide harder and more often with the walls — the pressure rises.

mcqs.q: Which expands the fastest on heating?
mcqs.why: Gas particles are far apart with very weak forces between them, so on heating they move much farther apart; solids, with tightly held particles, expand the least.

mcqs.q: A hot air balloon rises because the air inside it:
options: is heated, expands and becomes less dense than the cold air outside
is heavier than the outside air
mcqs.why: The expanded hot air is lighter (less dense); the upthrust of the surrounding denser air is then greater than the balloon's weight.

mcqs.q: A metal tyre is fixed tightly on a cart wheel by:
options: cooling the tyre so it expands
heating the tyre so it expands, fitting it on, then letting it contract and grip
mcqs.why: The heated ring expands enough to slip over the wheel; on cooling it contracts and grips the wheel firmly — a practical use of expansion and contraction.

mcqs.q: Water pipes may burst in severe winter because water:
options: expands on freezing, since ice takes more volume than water
mcqs.why: Water shows peculiar behaviour: below 4°C it expands, and expands further on freezing, so the ice can crack the pipe.

mcqs.q: Different substances expand at different rates because:
options: the forces between their particles and their arrangements differ
mcqs.why: Particles held by weak forces move apart more on heating than those held strongly; hence alcohol expands more than glass and brass more than iron.

lessons.title: Conductors, Insulators and Heat Transfer
lessons.notes_html:
Three Modes of Heat Transfer

Heat travels in three ways: conduction (through solids, particle to particle), convection (through liquids and gases by movement of particles) and radiation (through empty space by rays, e.g. heat from the Sun).

Good Conductors

Copper, aluminium, iron, steel and silver are good conductors of heat. That is why cooking utensils are made of these metals — heat passes quickly from the flame to the food.

Bad Conductors (Insulators)

Wood, plastic, glass, cork and wool (and still air) are bad conductors, or insulators, of heat. That is why pan handles are made of wood or plastic, so they do not burn our hands, and we wear woollen clothes in winter to keep body heat in.

Key Points

  • Heat transfers by conduction (solids), convection (liquids and gases) and radiation (empty space).
  • Metals such as copper, aluminium, iron, steel and silver conduct heat well.
  • Wood, plastic, glass, cork and wool are insulators used for handles and winter clothing.

mcqs.q: Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth by:
mcqs.why: Radiation transfers heat through empty space by rays, needing no medium — this is how the Sun's heat crosses space to the Earth.

mcqs.q: Conduction transfers heat mainly through:
mcqs.why: In conduction, heat passes from particle to particle through a solid without the particles themselves moving from place to place.

mcqs.q: Convection takes place in:
options: liquids and gases, by the movement of their particles
mcqs.why: In convection the heated particles of a liquid or gas themselves move and carry heat with them, setting up convection currents.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a good conductor of heat?
mcqs.why: Copper is an excellent conductor, which is why it is used in utensils and electric wires; wood, plastic and cork are insulators.

mcqs.q: Five good conductors of heat are:
options: wood, plastic, glass, cork and wool
rubber, air, wool, plastic and wood
glass, cork, paper, wood and plastic
copper, aluminium, iron, steel and silver
mcqs.why: These metals all conduct heat well and are used for cooking utensils and other heat-transfer purposes.

mcqs.q: Pan handles are made of wood or plastic because these materials are:
mcqs.why: Insulating handles stop the heat of the pan from reaching our hands, while the metal body of the pan conducts heat to the food.

mcqs.q: We wear woollen clothes in winter because wool:
options: is a bad conductor and keeps body heat from escaping
mcqs.why: Wool and the still air trapped in it are insulators, so body heat is retained and we feel warm.

mcqs.q: Cooking utensils are made of metals because metals:
options: conduct heat quickly from the flame to the food
mcqs.why: Metals are good conductors, so heat passes rapidly through the utensil walls and cooks the food evenly.

mcqs.q: Still air is a:
mcqs.why: Still air trapped in wool, fur and double glazing insulates well, which is why these keep us and our houses warm.

mcqs.q: Which list contains only bad conductors of heat?
options: wood, plastic, glass, cork and wool
mcqs.why: These non-metals are insulators used wherever heat flow must be blocked; the other lists contain only metals, which are good conductors.

lessons.title: Water Conservation and Irrigation
lessons.notes_html:
Conservation of Water

Conservation of water means saving water — using it carefully without waste, so that enough remains for the future.

Irrigation

Irrigation means supplying water to crops artificially through canals, wells, tube-wells or modern systems when rain is insufficient. In drip irrigation, water is delivered drop by drop through pipes and emitters directly at the roots of plants — it saves the most water, almost none is wasted by evaporation or flowing away, weeds grow less, and it works well in dry areas. In sprinkler irrigation, water is sprayed into the air through rotating sprinklers and falls on the field like rain; it covers a large area but loses more water by evaporation and wind. Drip irrigation is therefore more beneficial than sprinkler irrigation.

Rainwater Harvesting

Farmers should implement rainwater harvesting — collecting and storing rain water for later use. It recharges the underground water, raises the water table, provides water for irrigation in dry months, reduces flooding and soil erosion, and reduces dependence on canals and tube-wells. It is cheap and is the best answer to falling water levels.

Key Points

  • Conservation of water means saving water, not wasting it.
  • Drip irrigation delivers water drop by drop to the roots and wastes the least water.
  • Rainwater harvesting recharges groundwater and helps in dry months.

mcqs.q: Conservation of water means:
mcqs.why: Conservation means careful, non-wasteful use — saving water for present and future needs.

mcqs.q: Which type of irrigation is more beneficial, drip or sprinkler?
options: sprinkler, because it covers more area
drip, because it delivers water drop by drop to the roots with almost no waste
mcqs.why: Drip irrigation loses almost no water to evaporation or runoff and suppresses weeds, while sprinklers lose more water to wind and evaporation.

mcqs.q: Irrigation means:
options: supplying water to crops artificially when rain is insufficient
mcqs.why: Irrigation supplies water through canals, wells, tube-wells, drip or sprinkler systems to make up for insufficient rainfall.

mcqs.q: In sprinkler irrigation, water is:
options: delivered drop by drop at the roots
sprayed into the air and falls on the field like rain
mcqs.why: Rotating sprinklers spray water over a large area like rain, but more is lost to wind and evaporation than in drip irrigation.

mcqs.q: Rainwater harvesting helps farmers because it:
options: recharges underground water and raises the water table
mcqs.why: Stored rainwater seeps into the ground, raising the water table and providing irrigation water in dry months, while reducing floods and erosion.

mcqs.q: Drip irrigation is especially suitable for:
options: dry areas where water is scarce
mcqs.why: Because drip irrigation wastes almost no water, it works well where water is scarce and every drop matters.

mcqs.q: One disadvantage of sprinkler irrigation is that:
options: it uses no water at all
more water is lost by evaporation and wind
mcqs.why: Water sprayed into the air partly evaporates or blows away before reaching the roots, unlike drip irrigation.

mcqs.q: Rainwater harvesting reduces dependence on:
mcqs.why: Locally stored rainwater provides an independent supply, so farmers depend less on canal water and groundwater pumping.

mcqs.q: In drip irrigation, water reaches the plant through:
options: pipes and emitters placed at the roots
mcqs.why: Emitters release water drop by drop exactly at the roots, so almost all of it is used by the plant.

mcqs.q: Conservation of water at home can be done by:
options: fixing leaks and using water carefully
washing cars daily with a hose
mcqs.why: Saving water means avoiding waste — repairing leaks, closing taps and reusing water where possible.

lessons.title: Pickles and Food Preservation
lessons.notes_html:
Ingredients of Pickles

Mango pickle: raw (unripe) mango slices, table salt, turmeric powder, red chilli powder, mustard seeds/oil and other spices — honey is not used. Onion pickle: small peeled onions, vinegar (acetic acid) or mustard oil, table salt, red chilli powder, turmeric powder and mustard seeds. Lemon pickle: lemons, table salt, sugar, red chilli powder, turmeric powder and acetic acid (vinegar) as preservative — tea leaves are not used. Salt, oil, sugar and vinegar act as preservative agents; honey and pepper are not used as preservatives in these pickles.

Preparation

For mango pickle: wash raw mangoes, dry and cut into slices, remove the seeds; mix with salt and turmeric and keep for some hours so water is drawn out; drain, add chilli powder and spices, pack in a clean dry jar, pour heated and cooled mustard oil over until covered, and keep in sunlight for some days, shaking daily. Onion and lemon pickles are prepared in the same pattern — cleaned pieces mixed with salt, spices and vinegar/oil in a clean jar and matured for a few days. The oil forms a protective layer that keeps out air and germs, so a pickle prepared with mustard oil stays preserved for months.

Keeping Food Fresh

Food stays fresh when the growth of germs is stopped: by keeping it cold in refrigerators and freezers, by drying, by adding preservatives such as salt, sugar, oil and vinegar (as in pickles), by canning and vacuum packing, and by storing food in clean, dry, airtight containers. Refrigeration and deep freezing is the best technology for preserving meat, milk and fish, because low temperature stops the growth of germs; milk is also preserved by pasteurisation and by converting it into powder, cheese and yogurt.

Key Points

  • Salt, oil, sugar and vinegar preserve pickles; honey is not used in mango or lemon pickle.
  • Pickles mature in a clean jar kept in sunlight and shaken daily.
  • Cold storage (refrigeration/freezing) best preserves meat, milk and fish.

mcqs.q: While preparing pickles, which is NOT used as a preservative agent?
mcqs.why: Salt, vinegar (and oil and sugar) preserve pickles by stopping germ growth; honey is not used as a preservative in these pickles.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT used in making mango pickle?
mcqs.why: Mango pickle uses raw mango slices, salt, turmeric, chilli powder and mustard oil — honey has no place in it.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT used in the preparation of lemon pickle?
mcqs.why: Lemon pickle contains lemons, salt, sugar, chilli, turmeric and acetic acid (vinegar) as preservative; tea leaves are never used.

mcqs.q: The preservative used in lemon pickle is:
mcqs.why: Acetic acid (vinegar), together with salt, creates conditions in which germs cannot grow, preserving the pickle.

mcqs.q: In mango pickle, the salt is first mixed with the mango slices in order to:
options: draw out the water from the slices
mcqs.why: Salt draws water out of the mango pieces by osmosis; removing water helps preservation and prepares the slices for the spices and oil.

mcqs.q: The mustard oil poured over a pickle preserves it because it:
options: forms a protective layer that keeps out air and germs
mcqs.why: The oil seals the surface, cutting off air and germs, so the pickle stays preserved for months.

mcqs.q: The best technology to preserve meat, milk and fish is:
mcqs.why: Low temperature stops the growth of germs, so refrigeration and freezing preserve perishable foods like meat, milk and fish best.

mcqs.q: Milk is also preserved by pasteurisation, which means:
options: heating it and then cooling it rapidly to kill germs
mcqs.why: Pasteurisation heats milk to kill harmful germs and cools it quickly; milk is also preserved as powder, cheese and yogurt.

mcqs.q: Food stays fresh for a long time when:
options: it is kept warm and moist
the growth of germs is stopped by cold, drying, preservatives or airtight packing
mcqs.why: Germs spoil food; refrigeration, drying, salt/sugar/oil/vinegar, canning and vacuum packing all stop their growth.

mcqs.q: Onion pickle is prepared by keeping peeled onions in:
options: a spiced mixture of vinegar or mustard oil with salt, chilli, turmeric and mustard seeds
mcqs.why: The onions are covered with the spiced vinegar/oil mixture in a clean jar and kept for a few days, shaking daily, until pickled.

lessons.title: Juices and Technology in Daily Life
lessons.notes_html:
Preparation of Orange Juice

Wash fresh oranges, cut them in halves and squeeze out the juice with a juicer, removing the seeds. Add sugar to taste and a little clean water if the juice is too thick, and stir until the sugar dissolves. Serve fresh, adding ice if desired. The ingredients are oranges, sugar and water — garlic is never used in orange juice. Fresh juice should be used soon to keep its vitamins and taste.

Technology and Learning

Technology enhances students' learning: it gives access to digital books, educational videos, simulations and online libraries beyond the classroom; computers and the internet help in research, practice exercises and instant checking of answers; smart classes make difficult concepts easy through pictures and animations; and students can learn at their own pace and communicate with teachers anywhere.

Technology During COVID-19

During the COVID-19 pandemic, technology kept life going while people stayed home: online classes continued education; video calls kept families and offices connected; telemedicine allowed consultation with doctors; online shopping and banking reduced contact; thermal scanners, oximeters and ventilators helped in hospitals; and vaccine development and health apps were all technology-based.

Using a Thermometer

A classmate's temperature is checked with a clean clinical thermometer placed under the tongue (or in the armpit) for about one minute and read at eye level. A healthy person shows about 37°C (98.6°F). The thermometer must be washed or disinfected before each use.

Key Points

  • Orange juice = oranges + sugar + water; never garlic.
  • Technology supports learning through digital books, videos, simulations and online classes.
  • Normal body temperature is about 37°C (98.6°F).

mcqs.q: Which is NOT used in the preparation of orange juice?
mcqs.why: Orange juice is made from oranges, sugar and water (with ice if desired); garlic is never an ingredient of it.

mcqs.q: The correct preparation of orange juice is to:
options: boil the oranges for an hour
squeeze the juice from fresh oranges, remove the seeds, and add sugar and a little water
mcqs.why: Fresh oranges are halved and squeezed with a juicer; sugar to taste and a little water are stirred in, and the juice is served fresh.

mcqs.q: Fresh orange juice should be used soon because:
options: it loses its vitamins and taste if kept long
mcqs.why: Exposure to air and time destroys vitamins (especially vitamin C) and spoils the fresh taste of the juice.

mcqs.q: Technology enhances students' learning by giving them:
options: no need for teachers in any form
access to digital books, educational videos, simulations and online libraries
mcqs.why: Digital resources, smart classes and the internet let students research, practise and understand difficult concepts through pictures and animations.

mcqs.q: During the COVID-19 pandemic, education continued mainly through:
mcqs.why: With schools closed, technology — online classes, video calls, telemedicine, online banking and health apps — kept education and daily life running.

mcqs.q: Telemedicine during the pandemic allowed patients to:
options: consult doctors from home without visiting hospitals
mcqs.why: Telemedicine used phones and video calls for medical consultation, reducing contact and crowding in hospitals.

mcqs.q: A healthy classmate's temperature measured with a clinical thermometer is about:
mcqs.why: Normal human body temperature is about 37°C, which is 98.6°F on the Fahrenheit scale.

mcqs.q: Before using a clinical thermometer on another classmate, we must:
options: shake it hard for five minutes
mcqs.why: Cleaning and disinfecting the thermometer before each use prevents germs passing from one person to another.

mcqs.q: Smart classes make difficult concepts easy through:
mcqs.why: Visual presentations and simulations in smart classes help students see and understand concepts that are hard to grasp from text alone.

mcqs.q: Which hospital devices were technology-based helps during COVID-19?
mcqs.why: Thermal scanners detected fever, oximeters measured blood oxygen and ventilators supported breathing — key technologies in COVID-19 care.

lessons.title: Gravity, Mass and Weight
lessons.notes_html:
Gravity and Weight

An object is attracted towards the Earth due to gravity. Weight is the force of gravity acting on an object's mass. The Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of the Earth's gravity, so objects weigh one-sixth as much on the Moon: an object weighing 600 N on Earth weighs 600 ÷ 6 = 100 N on the Moon.

Jumping and Throwing on the Moon

With gravity six times weaker, the same effort carries a person about six times higher and farther. An athlete who can jump 5 metres up on Earth can jump about 5 × 6 = 30 metres on the Moon, and a shot put thrown 2 metres on Earth will travel about 2 × 6 = 12 metres on the Moon.

Mass and Weight of an Astronaut

When an astronaut travels from the Earth to the Moon, his mass remains exactly the same everywhere, because mass is the amount of matter in his body. His weight decreases: on the Moon it is about one-sixth of his weight on Earth. In deep space, far from any planet, he would feel almost weightless.

Key Points

  • Moon's gravity ≈ 1/6 of Earth's; weight on the Moon = Earth weight ÷ 6.
  • 600 N on Earth → 100 N on the Moon; a 5 m jump becomes about 30 m.
  • Mass never changes with place; weight changes with gravity.

mcqs.q: An object is attracted towards the Earth due to:
mcqs.why: Gravity is the Earth's gravitational pull that attracts every object towards the Earth.

mcqs.q: The weight of an object on Earth's surface is 600 N. Its weight on the Moon's surface will be:
mcqs.why: The Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of the Earth's, so weight on the Moon = 600 ÷ 6 = 100 N.

mcqs.q: An athlete can jump 5 metres up on the Earth. On the Moon he can jump about:
mcqs.why: With gravity six times weaker, the same effort lifts him about six times higher: 5 × 6 = 30 metres.

mcqs.q: A person throws a shot put 2 metres on Earth. The same throw on the Moon will carry it about:
mcqs.why: The shot weighs one-sixth as much and gravity pulls it down six times more weakly, so it travels about 2 × 6 = 12 metres.

mcqs.q: When an astronaut travels to the Moon, his mass:
mcqs.why: Mass is the amount of matter in the body and does not depend on place; only his weight changes with gravity.

mcqs.q: The Moon's gravity is about what fraction of the Earth's gravity?
mcqs.why: The Moon is much smaller and less massive than the Earth, so its surface gravity is about 1/6 of the Earth's.

mcqs.q: Weight is best defined as:
options: the amount of matter in a body
the force of gravity acting on a body's mass
mcqs.why: Weight is a force measured in newtons; it changes from planet to planet, unlike mass which stays constant.

mcqs.q: In deep space, far from any planet, an astronaut would:
options: feel almost weightless, though his mass is unchanged
mcqs.why: With no nearby planet's gravity pulling on him, his weight is nearly zero, but the matter in his body (mass) is the same.

mcqs.q: If an object weighs 300 N on Earth, its weight on the Moon is about:
mcqs.why: Weight on the Moon = Earth weight ÷ 6 = 300 ÷ 6 = 50 N.

mcqs.q: The unit of weight is the:
mcqs.why: Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons (N); the kilogram measures mass.

lessons.title: Tides
lessons.notes_html:
What Causes Tides?

The major cause of tides is the gravitational pull of the Moon. Although the Sun's total gravitational pull on the Earth is much greater, the Moon is very close to the Earth, and tides are caused by the difference of pull on the near and far sides of the Earth — which is stronger for the nearer body, the Moon.

Near Side and Far Side

The Moon's pull is strongest on the ocean water on the side facing the Moon (near surface), so that water bulges towards the Moon and produces a high tide there. On the far side the pull is weakest, so the water is left behind and bulges away from the Moon, producing the second high tide. Between the bulges are the low tides. The tides are highest during the full Moon, when the Sun, Moon and Earth are in line and their pulls combine.

Twice a Day

As the Earth rotates once a day, any coast passes through the two tidal bulges, so it experiences two high tides and two low tides — the sea washes in and out of beaches, shores and harbours twice a day, at intervals of about six hours. The Moon's gravity acts on everything on Earth, but its effect is noticeable only on the huge, free-moving masses of ocean water; solid land and small objects are held firmly and the difference of pull across them is far too small to move them.

Key Points

  • Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravitational pull and its difference across the Earth.
  • Two bulges (near and far sides) give two high tides daily; tides are highest at full Moon.
  • Only the oceans respond visibly because water can flow and collect into bulges.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the major cause of tides?
options: earthquakes on the surface of the ocean floor
mcqs.why: The Moon's gravity, and especially the difference of its pull across the Earth, raises the ocean bulges that we see as tides.

mcqs.q: The tides are highest during:
mcqs.why: At full Moon the Sun, Moon and Earth are in line, so the pulls combine and produce the highest (spring) tides.

mcqs.q: For producing tides, the Moon's pull is more effective than the Sun's because:
options: the Moon is bigger than the Sun
the Moon is very close to the Earth, so the difference of its pull across the Earth is greater
mcqs.why: Tides depend on the difference of pull between the near and far sides of the Earth; the nearby Moon produces a much bigger difference than the distant Sun.

mcqs.q: On the side of the Earth facing the Moon, the ocean water:
options: bulges towards the Moon, causing high tide
is pushed away, causing low tide
mcqs.why: The Moon's pull is strongest on the near-side water, drawing it into a bulge — a high tide — facing the Moon.

mcqs.q: A coast experiences two high tides in a day because:
options: the rotating Earth carries the coast through the two tidal bulges on opposite sides
mcqs.why: One bulge faces the Moon and the other is on the far side; as the Earth rotates once, each coast passes through both bulges and the two low-tide regions between them.

mcqs.q: High tides and low tides at a place occur at intervals of about:
mcqs.why: Two high and two low tides in 24 hours means a change roughly every six hours as the Earth rotates through the bulges.

mcqs.q: The Moon's gravity does not visibly move solid land and small objects because:
options: it acts only on water by nature
they are held firmly and the difference of pull across them is far too small
mcqs.why: The Moon's gravity acts on everything, but only the vast, free-moving oceans can flow and collect into bulges large enough to notice.

mcqs.q: The second high tide, on the side of the Earth away from the Moon, occurs because there the Moon's pull is:
options: weakest, so the water is left behind and bulges away from the Moon
mcqs.why: On the far side the pull is least, so the water lags behind the solid Earth and forms the second bulge opposite the Moon.

mcqs.q: Tides wash in and out of beaches and harbours:
mcqs.why: The statement is correct: two high tides (washing in) and two low tides (washing out) occur daily at most coasts.

mcqs.q: Which body is mainly responsible for the tides in Earth's oceans?
mcqs.why: Because of its closeness, the Moon's gravitational pull is the major cause of tides, even though the Sun's total pull on Earth is greater.

lessons.title: Seasons and the Tilt of the Earth
lessons.notes_html:
Why Seasons Occur

Seasons on the Earth's surface are caused by the tilt of the Earth on its axis together with its orbital motion around the Sun. Because of the tilt, each hemisphere leans towards the Sun for part of the year (its summer) and away from it for the other part (its winter).

Opposite Seasons in the Two Hemispheres

Pakistan is in the northern hemisphere and Australia in the southern hemisphere. When it is summer in Pakistan, the northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun and the southern hemisphere leans away, so it is winter in Australia. On 22nd June the southern hemisphere has winter, while the northern hemisphere has summer.

If the Earth Were Not Tilted

If the Earth's axis were not tilted, there would be no seasons. Every place would receive the same amount of sunlight throughout the year: the equator would always be hot, the poles always cold, and day and night would be equal (12 hours each) everywhere all year round.

Constellations and Stars

Constellations such as Ursa Major (Great Bear), Ursa Minor, Orion and Cassiopeia are patterns of stars as seen from Earth; they keep fixed patterns and appear to move across the sky during the night due to the Earth's rotation, and different constellations are visible in different seasons. A constellation is only an apparent pattern — its stars are not really grouped together — while a galaxy is a real, huge system of billions of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. Blue stars are much hotter and more massive, so they burn their fuel very fast and live shorter lives than yellow or red stars. Stars themselves are far too hot for life; life, if any, could exist only on suitable planets, and thousands of planets (exoplanets) have been discovered revolving around other stars.

Key Points

  • Seasons = Earth's axial tilt + its revolution around the Sun.
  • Summer in Pakistan means winter in Australia; 22 June is winter in the southern hemisphere.
  • Without the tilt there would be no seasons and day and night would always be 12 hours each.

mcqs.q: Seasons on the Earth's surface are caused by:
options: spin motion of the Earth about its own axis
orbital motion of the Earth around the Sun
tilt of Earth on its axis
the tilt of Earth and orbital motion of the Earth around the Sun
mcqs.why: Neither the tilt nor the revolution alone is enough: as the tilted Earth orbits the Sun, each hemisphere in turn leans towards the Sun and has summer.

mcqs.q: What is the season on 22nd June in the southern hemisphere?
mcqs.why: On 22 June the northern hemisphere leans most towards the Sun (its summer), so the southern hemisphere leans away and has winter.

mcqs.q: When there is summer in Pakistan, the season in Australia is:
mcqs.why: Pakistan is in the northern hemisphere and Australia in the southern; because of the axial tilt their seasons are opposite.

mcqs.q: If the Earth's axis were not tilted, then:
options: there would be no seasons and day and night would be equal all year
it would always be summer everywhere
mcqs.why: Without tilt, every place would receive the same sunlight throughout the year: equator always hot, poles always cold, 12-hour days everywhere.

mcqs.q: The Earth's spinning on its own axis causes:
mcqs.why: Rotation makes each place face the Sun and then turn away, giving day and night; seasons come from tilt plus revolution.

mcqs.q: A constellation differs from a galaxy because a constellation is:
options: a real group of billions of stars
only a pattern of stars as seen from Earth, not a real grouping
mcqs.why: The stars of a constellation lie at very different distances and are not physically grouped; a galaxy is a real system of billions of stars held by gravity.

mcqs.q: Blue stars have shorter lives than yellow or red stars because they:
options: are much hotter and more massive, so they burn their fuel very fast
mcqs.why: A blue star consumes its enormous fuel supply at a tremendous rate, exhausting it quickly; small red stars burn slowly and live far longer.

mcqs.q: Constellations appear to move across the night sky because of:
mcqs.why: The star patterns themselves stay fixed; our rotating Earth makes them seem to cross the sky during the night.

mcqs.q: Life cannot exist on the stars themselves because stars are:
mcqs.why: Stars are burning balls of gas at enormous temperatures; life, if it exists elsewhere, could only be on suitable planets around stars.

mcqs.q: Planets revolving around other stars are called:
mcqs.why: Thousands of exoplanets have been discovered orbiting other stars, though no life on them has been confirmed so far.
